chapters.summary: Council staff welcomes attendees to the Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection hearing, asks phones to be silenced, and instructs anyone wishing to speak to fill out an appearance card with the sergeants. Staff also says no one should approach the dais chair.
chapters.title: Council staff opens hearing and gives appearance-card instructions

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Hello, good morning.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Welcome to today's New York City Council hearing for the Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At this time, please silence all phones.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you wish to speak in today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with one of the sergeants.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Moving forward, no one is to approach the DA's chair.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may begin.

chapters.summary: Chair Harvey Epstein convenes the Consumer and Worker Protection hearing, identifies himself as chair, and recognizes Council Members Brewer and Schulman. He calls it the Council Member Brewer hearing and introduces pedicabs as for-hire vehicles.
chapters.title: Chair Epstein opens pedicab oversight hearing

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining the Consumer Worker Protection Hearing.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: My name is Harvey Epstein.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I'm the chair of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I'd like to recognize Councilmember Brewer and Councilmember Shillman, who is with me today.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We're calling this the Councilmember Brewer Hearing today.

chapters.summary: Epstein explains that pedicabs combine a bicycle with passenger carriages and generally serve tourists in Midtown, Times Square, and Central Park. He notes Council Member Brewer's connection to the issue.
chapters.title: Epstein describes pedicab operations in Midtown and Central Park

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Pedicabs are for hire vehicles that combine a bicycle seat, hand bars, and pedals for the driver with carriages for passengers.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Pedicabs operate generally, offer short-distance rides to tourists in Midtown and Councilmember Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Let's not forget about that.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Manhattan, particularly around Times Square as well as Central Park.

chapters.summary: Epstein says pedicabs are heavily regulated by DCWP but most operating cabs are unlicensed or unregistered. He notes an 850-plate cap, estimates 1,200–1,500 pedicabs on the street, and says only 275 valid plates appear in open data.
chapters.title: Epstein cites unlicensed pedicabs and low registration numbers

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Pedicabs are the most heavily regulated industry by DCWP, but these regulations mean very little when the vast majority of pedicabs operating in New York City are unlicensed, unregistered.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Despite the cap of 850 pedicab registered plates, there are estimated between 1,200 and 1,500 pedicabs operating in the city.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: An analysis on open data indicates there's just 275 valid pedicab registration plates, meaning that individuals who are choosing to operate unregistered pedicabs, even though they're available for pedicab plates.

chapters.summary: Epstein says enforcement falls to DCWP, NYPD, and Parks but mostly relies on criminal summonses. He reports that of 1,200 criminal pedicab summonses from 2025, only 9% resulted in punishment, with many dismissed or never prosecuted.
chapters.title: Epstein details ineffective criminal enforcement and summons dismissals

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Enforcement of pedicab regulations fall to DCWP, NYPD, and Parks, but the vast majority of enforcement is through criminal summons by NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: There are major concerns on how effective criminal enforcement is.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: The analysis of 1,200 criminal pedicab summons from 2025 found that 35%

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: 5% of the tickets were deemed legally insufficient.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: 25% were dismissed in the interest of justice.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: 20% were not pursued for other reasons.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: 9% were never prosecuted, and just 9% resulted in some kind of criminal or civil punishment.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: This status quo is not working for anyone.

chapters.summary: Epstein says the status quo fails tourists charged $500–$1,200 for short rides, Broadway productions disrupted by loud pedicab noise, and licensed drivers competing with unlicensed operators who avoid safety and insurance costs.
chapters.title: Epstein outlines harms to tourists, Broadway, and licensed drivers

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: It's not working for tourists who are routinely ripped off by unscrupulous pedicab drivers charged anywhere from $500 to $1,200 for a ride under 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: It's not working for the Broadway production that are interrupted by loud noise blaring from pedicabs outside their theaters.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And it's not working for licensed pedicabs who compete with unlicensed operators who do not invest in the city's safety equipment, insurance, or follow the rules.

chapters.summary: Epstein says the Midtown Community Justice Center convened a November 2025 roundtable with NYPD, DCWP, Central Park Conservancy, Manhattan DA, DOT, Times Square Alliance, and Broadway League. He notes the May 2026 report produced recommendations reflected in today's bills.
chapters.title: Epstein describes Midtown Justice Center roundtable and report

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Recognizing the system's not working, November 2025, the Midtown Community Justice Center, which adjudicates criminal summonses for pedicab violations,

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: organized a roundtable discussion with representatives from various stakeholders involved with the affected by the pedicab industry, including NYPD, DCWP, Central Park Conservancy, Manhattan DA's office, DOT, Times Square Alliance, and Broadway League.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: In May 26, the Justice Center published the report with goals of policy recommendations generated from stakeholders on the roundtable.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: A lot of those bills are being here today.

chapters.summary: Epstein lists Intros 64, 77, 673, 992, 993, 1026, and 1063, naming sponsors and topics including theater-district restrictions, timers, fares, meters, TLC authority, curb space, and electric assist. He says he looks forward to robust discussion.
chapters.title: Epstein introduces seven pedicab reform bills and sponsors

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Intro 64 by Councilmember Maloney related to restrictions on the operation of pedicabs in the theater district.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Intro 77 by Councilmember Brewer related to the visibility of rider timing in the pedicabs.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: 673 by Councilmember Wan related to the pedicab fares.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: 992 by Councilmember Brew related to the making certain changes to the pedicab law.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: 993 by Councilmember Brew related to establishing the taxi and limousine commission authority over pedicabs.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Intro 1026 by Councilmember Brew related to creating design curb space for pedicabs.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And 1063 by Councilmember Wilson related to pedicabs with electric assist.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I really look forward to a robust conversation about updating the pedicab laws, increasing compliance with pedicab regulations, and effective enforcement of pedicab businesses and drivers.

chapters.summary: Epstein invites the bill sponsors to speak and says he will start with Council Member Brewer.
chapters.title: Epstein invites bill sponsors to make statements

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And now I invite the bill sponsors to make a statement.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And obviously I'm going to start with Councilmember Brewer.

chapters.summary: Council Member Gale Brewer shares that she takes pedicabs at Central Park West and says drivers know not to overcharge her. She argues the city's approach has been inconsistent and ineffective and that the industry needs to start over.
chapters.title: Brewer says pedicab industry is not working and needs a restart

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Chair Epstein.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I am the only council member who takes pedicabs, and I take them at 72nd Street and Central Park West because I'm always late to get to the whatever speaking event is in the park.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But when I get there, they say, oh, it's Gail.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Don't overcharge her.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I do like that group of people, and I thank you for all the work that you do, but we do need regulation.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So thank you, Chair Epstein, for including the bills on today's agenda.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I think we heard that for too long the city's approach to the pedicab industry has been inconsistent and ineffective, creating problems for public safety, consumers, and drivers while burdening enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We've got to start over.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because nothing in this industry right now is working.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And New Yorkers and visitors and drivers all deserve better.

chapters.summary: Brewer credits Judge Wang and the Midtown Community Justice Center for initiating a pedicab task force with the New York Pedicab Alliance, Central Park Conservancy, Times Square Alliance, DA, and NYPD. She cites the report 'Fixing the Pedicab Problem' and says stakeholders still meet weekly.
chapters.title: Brewer credits Midtown Justice Center task force and report

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So last year, as you heard earlier, Judge Wang and his amazing staff at the Midtown Community Justice Center initiated a pedicab task force, including the New York Pedicab Alliance, the Central Park Conservancy, the Times Square Alliance,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: DA, NYPD, and many others, including our office, and they produced Fixing the Pedicab Problem.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That particular judge is awesome, and he's always trying to find ways to change policy as opposed to just doing what he does in the court.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So we took a hard look at what's not working.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And this report has clear and practical solutions.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We meet every single week still to talk about pedicabs.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Fixing the pedicab problem, a roadmap to reform has been helpful.

chapters.summary: Brewer says the city has about 850 authorized plates but 1,200–1,500 pedicabs operating, often with bogus credentials. She reports 172 pedicab complaints in 2025, with 86 involving overcharging and 35 unlicensed operators, and says tourists have been charged $500–$1,000 for 20-minute rides.
chapters.title: Brewer cites plate cap, overcharging complaints, and bogus credentials

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The report found, as you heard earlier, the city has approximately 850 authorized pedicab plates.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But an estimated, I don't know, 1,200 or 1,500 are operating by 2024 and probably more now.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They often have bogus credentials.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In 2025, there were 172 pedicab complaints, 311, half, 86, involved overcharging.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And another 35 involved unlicensed operators.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And there were probably more because often tourists don't complain.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We have heard that tourists have been charged $500 to nearly $1,000 for rides that are only 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So we need clearer rules.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Passengers need to know what they are being charged and who is responsible for the pedicab they are riding in.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: There are many legitimate drivers and businesses.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They should not have to compete with unlicensed operators and their predatory behavior.

chapters.summary: Brewer describes her bills on meters, moving oversight from DCWP to TLC, requiring third-party apps to carry liability insurance, and allowing pedicabs to use taxi relief stands. She says the goal is not to eliminate pedicabs but to make them safe, fair, and enforceable.
chapters.title: Brewer outlines meter, TLC transfer, insurance, and relief-stand bills

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So we have bills.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I have bills on meters, as you heard earlier, moving the oversight from Department of Consumer and Worker Protection to the Taxi and Limousine Commission.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Third party, these individuals, these apps to carry liability insurance.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And be able to use taxi relief stands if possible.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So those are just some of the bills and there are other ones being discussed today.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We're not trying to eliminate pedicabs because they are a form of transportation just like many others.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They're a part of New York City, particularly around Central Park, Times Square, Midtown, and the Theater District.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And the chair said he just saw one in his district on the Lower East Side.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We want legitimate drivers and businesses to operate safely and fairly.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We want passengers to know what they are paying.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Right now, you have no idea.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You just have to argue.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And the city has to be able to enforce the rules.

chapters.summary: Brewer thanks Judge John Wang, Danielle Mandis, Central Park Conservancy, Times Square Alliance, New York Pedicab Alliance, and her staff and legislative division. She calls the hearing long in the making and important.
chapters.title: Brewer thanks Judge Wang, advocates, and staff

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I definitely want to thank Judge John Wang.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Danielle Mandis, who is the Midtown Community Justice Center Director.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Betsy Smith and David Saltonstall from the Central Park Conservancy.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Tom Harris, Times Square Alliance, and Mekon Camera and Kenneth Winter for the New York Pedicab Alliance and many others.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: For my staff, former staff Sam Goldsmith started this whole discussion, and now Cynthia Hornig and Shula Puder are helping from my office, as well as the legislative division,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Margaret Lieford, Elliot Heisler, Neil Beckman, Wes Jones, Rachel Codoro, Sarah Swine, Natalie Meltzer, and Andrea Vasquez.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And I really appreciate this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's long in the making, and I think it's really important.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And thank you very much.

chapters.summary: Epstein thanks Brewer and, seeing no other sponsor statements, turns to the agency panel. Staff administers the affirmation, and Epstein introduces Carlos Ortiz, Haley Radiker, and Ira Goldapper.
chapters.title: Epstein swears in DCWP and TLC officials

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And seeing no other people to issue voting statements, we're going to turn it over to the agency and get them sworn in.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before this committee and to respond honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Okay, and so here we have Carlos Ortiz, Deputy Commissioner, Hilly Radiker, Associate Commissioner, and Ira Goldapper, who is a Deputy Commissioner for Uniformed Services.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We have on Zoom, Council Member...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Adderball and Councilmember Hanks has joined us in person.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Please begin whenever you're ready.

chapters.summary: Carlos Ortiz introduces himself as DCWP Chief of Staff, joined by Haley Radiker and Ira Goldapper of TLC. He says DCWP is the licensing agency for pedicab businesses and drivers and registers pedicab vehicles.
chapters.title: DCWP Chief of Staff Carlos Ortiz introduces agency role in pedicab licensing

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Epstein and members of the Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: My name is Carlos Ortiz, and I am the Chief of Staff of the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I am joined by our Associate Commissioner of Intergovernmental Affairs, Haley Radiker, as well as my colleague, Ira Goldapper, Deputy Commissioner for Uniformed Services Bureau at the Taxing and Museum Commission.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: The New York City Department of Consumer Worker Protection is the nation's leading municipal enforcement agency charged with delivering economic justice.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: In New York City, we are also the licensing agency for both pedicab businesses and drivers.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And we register pedicab vehicles as well.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: There are currently 130 active pedicab business licensees associated with 330 registered pedicab vehicles and approximately 600 active pedicab driver licenses.

chapters.summary: Ortiz says there are 130 active pedicab business licensees, 330 registered vehicles, and about 600 active driver licenses, with a city cap of 840 vehicles. He says DCWP enforces pricing disclosure and annual compliance checks, while NYPD and Parks handle on-street enforcement, and noncompliance remains a problem.
chapters.title: Ortiz reports 330 registered vehicles, 600 driver licenses, and noncompliance

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Pedicab businesses are only allowed to operate a registered pedicab vehicle with a licensed pedicab driver.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: A pedicab business can have up to 30 registered vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: However, the total number of pedicab vehicles allowed to be registered with

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: The city is capped at 840 vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: DCGP enforces rules regarding pricing and disclosure to consumers, as well as conducts annual compliance checks on pedicabs for issues like cap conditions, rate signage, and license disclosures.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: On-treat enforcement of pedicab activity is conducted by the NYPD or by the Parks Department if the activity is occurring in parkland.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Over the past three years, our sister agencies have issued approximately 5,000 summonses to pedicabs for illegal activity.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Candidly, in recent years, the pedicab industry has struggled with noncompliance, including unlicensed activity.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: This not only impacts consumers, but also the businesses that want to be in compliance and who engage hundreds of workers.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: DCAP and our sister agencies have worked closely with each other.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And key community stakeholders to coordinate enforcement and educational activities to support this industry.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: This includes the development of educational literature, outreach initiatives, working closely with local associations such as the New York Pedicab Alliance, and standing up a Central Park task force for the enforcement activities referenced above.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We remain committed to working with our partners to come together on common sense solutions for this industry.

chapters.summary: Ortiz says Intro 64 would prohibit pedicabs from stopping, standing, or picking up/dropping off within 50 feet of theater entrances in the theater district and require DOT signage. He notes pedicabs already face curb regulations and defers to DOT and NYPD.
chapters.title: Ortiz testifies on Intro 64 theater-district pedicab restrictions

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Turning to today's legislation, Introduction 64 prohibits pedicab drivers from parking, stopping, or standing a pedicab or picking up or dropping off passengers within 50 feet of any entrance or exit of a theater located in the theater district zone.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: It would also require the Department of Transportation to post signs or other markings indicating the areas in which such pedicab restrictions are applicable.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Pedicabs are already subject to all existing curb regulations for vehicles, such as existing no standing space.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: signage.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Most theaters have no standing signs already, and there is an established process for a theater to request a no standing signage.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: If there happens to be any locations that do not have it already.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We defer to our colleagues at DOT and NYPD for further considerations regarding this bill.

chapters.summary: Ortiz says Intro 77 would require timers affixed to the rear of the bicycle seat within clear view of passengers. DCWP supports the bill as a way to reduce consumer deception and assist on-street enforcement.
chapters.title: Ortiz supports Intro 77 requiring visible pedicab timers

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Instruction 77 will require that the timer and pedicabs be affixed to the rear of the bicycle seat, within clear view of all pedicab passengers.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: DCVP supports this bill.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We share Council's concerns related to consumer deception and scams for pedicab riders.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We believe this legislation would not only assist consumers against overcharges, but also on-street enforcement agencies against bad actors.

chapters.summary: Ortiz says Intro 673 would require DCWP to set fixed per-minute pedicab rates indexed to inflation. DCWP supports better price clarity but warns price controls may burden the agency and compliant businesses, and wants to hear from stakeholders.
chapters.title: Ortiz supports price clarity but questions fixed-rate price controls

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Introduction 673 would require DCVP to set fixed per minute rates for pedicab rides indexed to inflation.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: DCVP supports bringing better price clarity to consumers, particularly in the context of consumer deception and overcharges reported in this industry.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: However, price controls can also be an overly burdensome measure for the agency to set, as well as for businesses that are otherwise complying with the law.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Today, we are interested to hear from business and worker stakeholders to understand the implications of price controls on their take-home pay and ability to operate.

chapters.summary: Ortiz says Intro 992 would require meters, scannable registration plates, safety training, removal of imprisonment, and a ban on illegal noise devices. DCWP supports the intent but says it lacks street-safety expertise for training and is evaluating scannable plate costs.
chapters.title: Ortiz supports meter intent but raises safety-course and plate-cost concerns

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Introduction 992 would require pedicabs to have meters to calculate the price of pedicab rides and registration plates with a scannable code that displays the pedicab registration number and business name.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: The bill would also require pedicab drivers to take a safety training developed by DCVP in order to obtain or renew a license.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: It would remove imprisonment for pedicab-related violations and specify that a pedicab driver may not use any device that makes illegal noise.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: DCDAP supports the intent of this legislation.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Requiring a meter would improve the consumer experience in this industry, especially for greater pricing clarity.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Imprisonment should not be a penalty for pedicab-related violations, and devices that make illegal noise should be explicitly prohibited.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: However, other facets of this bill raise concerns for the agency.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: In particular, we do not have street safety expertise to develop a safety course that would be adequate for drivers.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Additionally, we are evaluating the potential high cost to mandating scannable registration plates.

chapters.summary: Ortiz says Intro 1063 would allow pedicabs with electric motors under 750 watts and pedal assistance limited at 15 mph or a DOT-set speed. He says NYPD is concerned that pedal assist is difficult to enforce in the field, and the administration is ready to work with the Council.
chapters.title: Ortiz notes NYPD concerns over enforcing electric pedal assist

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Instruction 1063 would allow pedicabs to be equipped with an electric motor of less than 750 watts that limits pedaling assistance when the pedicab reaches a speed of 15 miles per hour or any other speed determined by the Department of Transportation by rule.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: The New York City Police Department is concerned that allowing pedal assist will be problematic because it's very difficult for the officer to enforce this in the field.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify before your committee on today's legislation.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We look forward to hearing from all relevant stakeholders today.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And the administration stands ready to work with the council, stakeholders, and all our partners across city government to support a vibrant and robust pedicab industry that protects consumers, workers, and small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I'll turn it over to my colleague at TLC.

chapters.summary: Ira Goldapper introduces himself as TLC Deputy Commissioner for the Uniformed Services Bureau. He says TLC regulates about 180,000 licensed drivers and 115,000 vehicles, conducts over 110,000 inspections, and issues about 24,000 patrol summonses annually.
chapters.title: TLC Deputy Commissioner Ira Goldapper describes TLC licensing and enforcement scale

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Epstein and members of the Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to provide testimony on behalf of the New York City Taxi and Limousine Commission.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: My name is Ira Goldapper and I serve as TLC's Deputy Commissioner for the Uniformed Services Bureau.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: TLC regulates New York City's taxi and for hire vehicle industries, including approximately 180,000 licensed drivers and 115,000 vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Together, TLC licensees provide nearly 1 million trips each day.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: With approximately 440 employees, TLC carries out significant licensing, inspection, and enforcement responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: In fiscal year 2026, we conducted more than 110,000 inspections, received over 29,000 complaints, and issued approximately 24,000 patrol summonses.

chapters.summary: Goldapper says Intro 1026 would let pedicabs use existing taxi and FHV relief stands and require 15 new pedicab-only stands in Midtown. TLC does not support expanding existing stands because 180,000 TLC drivers already share 107 stands, though it agrees workers need rest space.
chapters.title: Goldapper opposes sharing taxi relief stands with pedicabs

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: I would like to briefly address two bills before the committee today.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Intro 1026 would allow pedicabs to use existing taxi and for hire vehicle relief stands and require DOT to establish 15

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: additional relief stands in Midtown Manhattan exclusively for pedicabs.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Taxi and FHV relief stands provide drivers with free, legal parking so that they can use a

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: bathroom, eat a meal, and take a necessary break during their shifts.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Approximately 180,000 TLC licensed drivers currently have access to 107 relief stands citywide.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: There is significant demand for curb space throughout the city, particularly in midtown Manhattan, where pedicab activity is concentrated, and space is especially limited.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: TLC believes it is important to consider the existing demand for taxi and FHV relief stands as the Council evaluates this proposal.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: TLC does not support expanding the use of existing taxi and FHB relief stands to pedicabs, but concurs with the underlying premise of the bill that workers should have more space to rest on our city streets.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: These spaces are limited and already in high demand.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: And adding additional users would further constrain access to needed rest space for taxi and FHV drivers.

chapters.summary: Goldapper says Intro 993 would transfer pedicab regulation from DCWP to TLC. He argues pedicabs operate under a different model, the transfer would be extremely costly, and TLC does not believe it is the best path forward, though it will share expertise.
chapters.title: Goldapper says TLC transfer would be costly and not best path

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Intro 993 would transfer responsibility for regulating pedicabs from the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection to TLC.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: TLC's current regulatory framework is designed around the taxi and for hire vehicle industries.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Pedicabs operate under a different model and regulatory framework.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Including different vehicle types,

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: rating patterns and applicable laws.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: The concerns raised regarding the pedicab industry, including unlicensed activity and quality of life issues, are important and warrant careful consideration.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Any potential changes to the existing regulatory structure should be evaluated

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: in the context of the expertise and operational needs of the agencies involved.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: This legislation would be extremely costly to implement, going well beyond existing resources.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: TLC remains committed to working with DCWP, DOT, the Council, and other partners

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: to share our regulatory and enforcement expertise and support the development of an alternative approach to these issues as we do not believe this bill is the best path forward.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Together, excuse me, thank you Chair Epstein and members of the committee for the opportunity to provide TLC's perspective.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: We look forward to continuing to work with the council and our agency partners.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks about the 24,000 violations mentioned by TLC. Goldapper clarifies those are taxi-related, and Epstein turns to the roughly 1,200 pedicab violations and why fewer than 10% result in penalties.
chapters.title: Epstein questions TLC and DCWP on pedicab summons outcomes

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you both.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And I know we've been joined by council members De La Rosa, Maloney, and Ariola online.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And I know we're going to get into some questioning.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I just, so let me just talk about.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: The violation, you mentioned 24,000 violations have been issued.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: How many of those resulted in some kind of fine penalty or sanction of 24,000?

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Are you referring to the 24?

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Are you asking about pedicab violations?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, you said there are 24,000.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Those are related to taxi.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

chapters.summary: Epstein says if tickets are meaningless there is no incentive to comply. He asks what DCWP is doing to improve compliance and prevent tourists from being ripped off, noting not everyone can be Gale Brewer.
chapters.title: Epstein presses DCWP on low follow-through for pedicab enforcement

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So we talked earlier about 1,200 pedicab violations in the last year, and it seems like some less than 10% issue, there's some kind of...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Action where there's an ongoing problem.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: What's happening there?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Why is it so low?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: What's going on with the enforcement actions that we're seeing on the ground that don't result in any kind of follow through?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Thank you for that question, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think with respect to pedicab enforcement,

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: on street enforcement handled by the police department or the parks department if it's happening in parkland.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And my understanding is over the past three years, they've issued approximately 5,000 summonses to pedicab operators.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: In terms of the pathway and what it takes and what happens to the adjudications, I don't have insight into that.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: But we can get that information from the police department.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks DCWP what it is doing to move the industry toward legal standards and protect consumers. He emphasizes that tourists are vulnerable and that the agency is the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection.
chapters.title: Epstein presses DCWP on compliance and tourist protection

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, honestly, if people think a ticket's meaningless, then there's no incentive to comply with the law if there's no incentive to comply with the law, right?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: What's DCWP doing about that?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You had staff at this roundtable.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You've heard the facts.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You've seen the report.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: What are we doing about better compliance?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: to make sure we move an industry to a more legal standard.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I mean, we don't want tourists coming here getting ripped off.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You know, we all can't be Gail Brewer when we get on in a paddy cab.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So how are we going to ensure that people are being protected?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You're the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection.

chapters.summary: Ortiz acknowledges noncompliance is serious and unfair to compliant businesses. He describes coordinated enforcement with sister agencies, summonses, confiscations, police trainings, weekly reports on licensed actors, and updated driver licenses to reduce falsification.
chapters.title: Ortiz details coordinated enforcement, trainings, and weekly reports

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Thank you for that question, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And I want to echo also the sentiments raised earlier in the opening statements that noncompliance is a serious problem, particularly for businesses that are following the rules.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And I think it's inherently unfair that a business that follows the rules in one situation feels that others are getting away scot-free.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: But for that reason, we have been working closely with our sister agencies to stand up coordinated enforcement activities.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: That includes summonses.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: That also includes, at times, confiscations.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: That includes trainings that we provide to the police officers.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We also provide weekly reports to our sister agencies so they are aware of who the licensed actors are.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And ideally identify quicker who the unlicensed actors are.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We've also worked to update even what could seemingly sound like a minuscule thing, but updating the driver license, the pedicab driver license that drivers receive so it's harder to falsify.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We've been working on these initiatives throughout the past three years, candidly,

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: with our sister agencies in a measure to address compliance.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: That also ties into what we've been doing newly in this past year, in this administration, which is creating deeper ties with stakeholders.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: insurers met multiple times now with, to call out a few names, the New York Pedicab Alliance, the Times Square bid, the Broadway Association, because we recognize that this is an issue that still requires more attention from the city.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And from our perspective, this hearing is an opportunity for all of us, and especially the stakeholders, to raise those concerns because we do want to come up with solutions.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks whether the situation is better than three years ago or solved. Ortiz says the issue is not solved and points to legislation on pricing clarity and continued enforcement coordination as partial solutions.
chapters.title: Epstein asks if pedicab problem is solved; Ortiz says no

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, but what, I mean, I know you said you've kind of in the last three years moved forward in trying to improve the situation.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Do you think today the situation is better than it was three years ago?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Do you think this issue is solved?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: It seems like no one thinks we've at a place where we have appropriate solutions, especially on the ticketing and illegal pedicabs are out on the street.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think the issue, I mean, I think we're all aware that the issue is not solved.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think there are legislation on today's docket that we are supportive of that we want to make sure can be implemented, particularly around greater pricing clarity and disclosures to consumers.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And I think there are measures that we can continue taking with our sister agencies on the enforcement side to ensure that enforcement is equitable and focused on the bad actors of the industry.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks how many pedicab confiscations have occurred in the past three years. Ortiz says he does not have exact numbers because NYPD handles confiscations, but DCWP participates in coordinated enforcement that sometimes results in confiscation.
chapters.title: Epstein questions DCWP on pedicab confiscations

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You mentioned confiscation.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: How many confiscations of pedicabs have happened in the past three years?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't have the exact numbers on number of confiscations.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Those are handled by the New York City Police Department.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Can you get back to us with that information, please?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So you know they've happened?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Yes, they do conduct.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We have been participating in coordinated activities around enforcement where confiscations are the result.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: You know, the agency, the CCP, does not have the capacity or ability to do confiscation, so we work with the police department to do that work.

chapters.summary: Epstein describes a tourist taking a 20-minute pedicab ride and being charged $1,000. He asks what recourse DCWP offers and how a consumer can know which pedicab is legal among many.
chapters.title: Epstein asks what recourse exists for overcharged pedicab passengers

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So what do you say to a consumer who's, like, took a 20-minute cab ride, pedicab ride, and it cost them $1,000?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: What recourse does DCWP have in place to help that consumer, whether a tourist or a New Yorker, out in that situation?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think to a certain extent, in any situation when we're dealing with unlicensed actors, I think the message that we have to communicate to consumers is preventative.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Engaging with unlicensed actors, whether that's a home improvement contractor or a pedicab, it's particularly dangerous for a consumer because there is limited recourse because these actors can escape the ability for enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I would say that if a consumer is engaging with a pedicab to be sure that it's licensed, to ensure that they're capturing the license information, the rate signage, and that they provide that information to the agency so that we can mediate.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And if we see a pattern of complaints happening with a particular business or driver, then we can investigate.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So, you know, someone, let's say it's a tourist, comes to New York.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: They go to Central Park and they are like, oh, I'm going to get on a paddy cab.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So they get on a pedicab.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: They don't know what's legal or not because there's 40 pedicabs sitting right there, and they just choose one to get on.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And then at the end of the 20-minute ride, the guy or woman says, you know, $500.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You know, how is that person ever going to have the information you're suggesting to be able to make that good faith argument?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And what do they do after they've paid when they've figured out that they've been ripped off?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Like, what is DCWP doing to ensure that person who's been ripped off gets some kind of recourse?

chapters.summary: Ortiz says DCWP distributed information through hotels, tourism partners, and park signage, especially during the World Cup season. He says tourists often write off scams or do not follow up, making complaints hard to action, and supports pricing clarity legislation.
chapters.title: Ortiz describes consumer education and difficulty following up on complaints

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Thank you for that question, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think what we worked over the past summer, particularly in the peak of the World Cup season, was to distribute as much information out as possible to consumers and tourists regarding their rights when they're using these services.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And that included working with the Hotel Association, New York City Tourism, creating signage in New York City parks with our Parks Department colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: If a tourist has an issue where that comes up, where they feel they've been scammed or overcharged, or the pricing was inaccurate based on what they received, they can bring that to us.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think there are challenges, though, with that in the sense that a tourist, I think, unfortunately, we have a situation where tourists kind of write it off.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And unfortunately, they don't provide us all the information we need, or also when we reach out to them, they don't follow up with us.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: It makes it very difficult.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And I think ideally some aspects of the legislation on today's docket would improve that pricing clarity and improve how much a consumer could be charged in the first place, which I think would be beneficial for the industry.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And even we could think of an industry where we are not just serving tourists, but we're serving New Yorkers as well.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think that is the ultimate goal we have to have in the city for the pedicab industry.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: But that would require, to your point, a stricter regime with stricter compliance measures for bad actors.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks how many pedicab complaints DCWP has received and how many overall complaints went to NYPD and DEP. He requests data on outcomes, resolutions, and whether consumers received money back.
chapters.title: Epstein requests complaint counts and outcomes from DCWP, NYPD, DEP

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Well, how many complaints have been filed about pedicabs with your agency?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Over this past nine months, we've

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: received approximately 135 complaints.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: That is not the totality of complaints the city receives, however.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Ours would typically be around overcharging or pricing, but if a complaint is related to motorized activity or unlicensed activity or something dangerous happening in the street, that would be routed to the police department.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And do you know how many overall complaints for the last nine months, including the overpricing and the other ones, other through one complaints that might be directed to other agencies?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I don't have information on what complaints the police department receives.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I would say since 2022.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And Carl, can you get that for us?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I would say since 2022, the agency has received 335 overcharged complaints.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And so beyond you and the NYPD, there are other agencies that are going to funnel complaints or pedicabs as well?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I believe that the majority of the complaints would go to the police department.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I don't believe that complaints go to the Parks Department.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: How about loud music?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Would that go to DEP?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: DEP is, yes, also involved in that, but those could also be sent to the police department, too, because they have the ability to enforce on that.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So could you get us all the complaint numbers?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: How many went to DEP?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: How many went to the NYPD?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: How many went to DCWP?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And what those bucket outcomes are?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Were they resolved?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: They were, you know, disclosed?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Like, you know, and of your complaints, how many resulted in people getting money back?

chapters.summary: Ortiz says over the past year DCWP could not action any complaints because of missing information or consumers not following up. Epstein notes that means zero follow-through on 135 complaints, and Ortiz says the agency immediately reaches out but lacks data on responses.
chapters.title: Ortiz says DCWP could not action pedicab complaints due to missing information

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I can speak to over the past year that we've not been able to action on any of the complaints we've received because either the lack of information that we've been provided or consumers not following up when we reached out to them.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So of the 135, we've got zero that there's any follow through on.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Well, I would push back on that slightly.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We do follow through.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We immediately reach out to the consumer, and it is a priority for us to make sure that consumer hears from us.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: In terms of actioning on the complaint subsequently, that we have not been able to get.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Of those complaints, how many did the consumer actually respond wanting to get redress?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think the issue with the complaints is either we don't have enough information to contact the consumer, or when we reach out to the consumer, they do not respond to us.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: But some do respond, right?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I don't think we have, we don't have data saying that somebody responded, but I can double check that for you.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

chapters.summary: Epstein turns to TLC and asks about its street operations enforcement. Goldapper says TLC targets unlicensed for-hire operations across all five boroughs and airports, focusing on hotspots, but says regular enforcement against bad actors is difficult citywide.
chapters.title: Epstein asks TLC about street enforcement operations

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Just to turn our attention to TLC.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So can you talk about your street operations enforcement under TLC licensing?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And so we understand what you're actually doing on the street.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Because we hear from DCWP that basically they have no street-facing operation.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: They rely on NYPD, but you do have a street-facing operation, right?

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: We do.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: We target unlicensed for hire operations.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: with respect to taxis and for hire vehicles across all five boroughs that include as well as airports.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: There are major hotspots in, like I said, each of the boroughs, shopping centers, the major transportation hubs.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: It's a large city to cover, and we do our best to hit that.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: But one of the big pieces is that for effective unlicensed for higher activity enforcement, you have to hit

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: the same bad actors with such regularity that it becomes cost prohibitive for them to continue to operate.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: And that's something that is, it's difficult to cover all five boroughs.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks how many violations TLC issued this year for illegal operations. Goldapper says TLC issued over 5,000 summonses for unlicensed operators and 790 for illegal street hails, but cannot yet provide summons-by-summons outcomes due to OATH delays.
chapters.title: Epstein questions TLC on 5,000 unlicensed-operator summonses and outcomes

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And you said how many violations have you issued this year for illegal operations?

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: So calendar year to date, we've issued over 5,000 summonses for unlicensed operators, as well as 790 summonses for illegal street hails.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And then of those 5,000, how many of those resulted in some kind of...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Actualized civil penalty or actions resulting in either termination of a license or some other enforcement action?

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: So I don't have the specific numbers because of the, there is a delay between the issuance of the summons and when it gets through oath.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: And we can look to get somewhat of a breakdown for you, but because of that gap, it won't be summons for summons.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: We can give you that sort of general percentages.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Do you have 25 data?

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: I believe I do.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Let me please check.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Not just the overall number, but also how many resulted in enforcement?

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we have our summonses related to the field summonses are not broken down into the type of summons.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: We can look to do that and get those numbers for you.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks how many TLC staff issue summonses on the streets. Goldapper says the enforcement division has about 130 officers, with about 85 in street enforcement, far fewer than needed to end unlicensed for-hire activity.
chapters.title: Epstein asks how many TLC officers conduct street enforcement

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, so how many people do you have issuing summonses?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: How many people are out on the streets of New York?

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: So the enforcement division within TLC's Uniformed Services Bureau has about 130 officers, including supervisors, managers, trainers, investigators.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: How many would be street enforcement staff?

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: So about 85.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: 85 for the city?

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So it's 85 more than DCWP.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: But far fewer, but far less than needed to end unlicensed for hire activity within the taxi and for hire vehicle.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: That's a good budget conversation for us in the spring for sure, to make sure that we want to make it fair for people who are, you know, getting unlicensed, who are protected from unlicensed vehicles.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks whether TLC inspectors in Times Square could enforce illegal taxi and pedicab violations with the same staff. Goldapper says TLC does not know the pedicab industry and that enforcement alone is not a panacea; education and stakeholder engagement are also needed.
chapters.title: Epstein asks whether TLC inspectors could also enforce pedicab laws

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Just one more question for you, if I could.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So increased enforcement, increased authority on enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Could those same inspectors, if they're sitting in

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Times Square, do enforcement for an illegal cab or illegal TLC cab, or an illegal pedicab?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Could they be, and that person could actually do the same thing, or you'd have to hire a separate division of people to do pedicabs?

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Well, it's somewhat of a difficult question, given the complexities.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: We do not know the pedicab industry.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Something you can learn, obviously.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: People can learn.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: One thing to keep in mind is we don't believe...

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Enforcement alone is sort of the panacea to the industry.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: We've learned that with our own experience in enforcing against unlicensed for hire activity.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: It requires significant education for the public, for one, to try to remove the demand for unlicensed activity.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: As well as an understanding and stakeholder engagement with the industries to understand what are the barriers for entry, what's precluding individuals from actually getting licensed and doing what they're supposed to be doing,

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: and getting to those root causes.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: So it's more than just enforcement in order to achieve the results.

chapters.summary: Epstein notes most pedicab users are tourists who are not in New York long enough to learn local rules. He asks what tools TLC would use for education if enforcement alone is not the answer.
chapters.title: Epstein questions TLC on educating tourists about pedicabs

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So how would you do education in this industry on the pedicabs?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Obviously, a vast majority of the people using them aren't New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: They are people who are coming in, whether driving in or flying in.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: They're not here for extended periods of time.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: What tools would you have to do that kind of education that you're referencing if you're saying enforcement isn't going to be the answer to this problem?

chapters.summary: Ortiz says DCWP builds ties with the industry, works with the Hotel Association and NYC Tourism, canvasses Central Park, and uses social media to educate tourists. He says the goal is an ecosystem of information rather than one tool.
chapters.title: Ortiz details DCWP outreach to hotels, tourism, and social media

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Let me take that question to recap kind of the educational initiatives we've been taking.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Because I hear your point.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think that is a difficulty when there's a moving group that's not based in the city.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: So what we've tried to leverage is...

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I guess really a relational aspect to this, creating deep ties with the industry to make sure they understand their obligations for compliance, but also so they can help disseminate the educational materials that we've developed for tourists in general, but also in pedicabs in particular.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We've worked also with, for example, the Hotel Association, New York City Tourism.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We've also done canvases of certain areas of the city, like Central Park, to meet consumers directly.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And we've also been trying to leverage as much as possible for tourists coming to the city, our social media footprint, which we've been expanding in the past nine months, to showcase our partnership with the industry and the obligations of the industry, too.

chapters.summary: Epstein says tourists are unlikely to check DCWP social media before taking a pedicab in another city. Ortiz agrees no single tool works and says DCWP's six-person outreach team reached nearly 100,000 New Yorkers and 30,000 people in the streets over the summer.
chapters.title: Epstein challenges social-media education; Ortiz cites field outreach

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Just to, and I'm going to, I know my colleagues have questions too, but to be honest, so

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: When I'm visiting another city and I'm going to do a tourist-related thing, probably the last thing I'm doing is going to DCWP's social media page and be like, what is the industry?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: It's not a realistic scenario to say, I'm going to go to Prague and I'm going to get on a bus and I'm going to figure out what the city agency in a language I probably don't speak is going to say about what the rules are around.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: It just, I just, it belies like.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Well, I would say that any one of those tools by itself is not going to work.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: But the purpose of using all these different tools is to create an ecosystem where we're trying to get this information out.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: It is a process.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I've done community fairs now 10 years of my career, and it's hard work.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: You're physically in the field trying to talk to people in real-time settings.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Not to say it's always perfect, but we work at it.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Well, that's something like that physically in the field where people are, where these hubs are, is a really good way of getting to people instead of like using social media.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Like, unfortunately, it's a staffing requirement, but it might be something that might really be beneficial to have people out and about, especially in areas where we see high concentrations of this issue happening.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We do, and we ourselves conduct an immense amount of outreach.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And just this year, I'd like to say that, or I consider that our outreach team is probably the best outreach team in the city.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And just this year, with a team of six, we've been able to reach nearly 100,000 New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Over the summer, reach...

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: 30,000 people in the streets about worker rights and consumer rights, particularly in the peak of the tourist season.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We have been, myself and Haley, have been on the ground at Central Park and the theater district to talk to pedicab folks, to talk to tourists in the streets.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: So it is work that we are actively putting in every day.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Council Member Carl Wilson asks whether the 840-vehicle cap is reached; Ortiz says only 330 are registered and perhaps 1,200 are unregistered. Wilson asks what violations can revoke a license, and Ortiz says adjudicated violations or voided insurance can lead to suspension or revocation.
chapters.title: Wilson questions DCWP on registration cap and license revocation

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I want to turn it over to some of my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I know Councilmember Wilson and then Councilmember Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So you said, sorry, I missed your testimony, but I'm reading it here, that the number of pedicab vehicles is capped at 840.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Are we at that cap?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Currently, there are 330 registered vehicles with the city.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: How many do you suspect are not registered?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: My understanding of some of the public reporting out there, that there could be approximately 1,200 unlicensed or unregistered vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And when a vehicle license is issued, there are terms which would cause them to lose that license, right?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: And what are some of those?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Are things like noise or traffic violations part of what you would use to revoke a license?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: It would be a certain number of violations adjudicated over a period of time that would allow us to go and try to revoke or suspend a license.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: But do you see...

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Go ahead, please finish.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Additionally, there are certain requirements specifically in this industry related to, for example, insurance.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And in the case of an insurance of a pedicab business is...

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Is voided for any particular reason, we would void the license as well.

chapters.summary: Wilson notes DCWP does not receive direct reports of on-street infractions from NYPD or DEP, so it cannot enforce against bad actors. Ortiz says DCWP coordinates with police and parks but does not get adjudication outcomes, and Wilson suggests another agency may be better equipped.
chapters.title: Wilson presses DCWP on lack of NYPD infraction reporting

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: But DCWP doesn't get the direct reports of infractions, right?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: You said like DEP is called to some, NYPD is called to some.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: That's correct, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: The on-street enforcement is handled by the police department.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And in terms of the summons information, we don't receive it directly.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So do you speak with them?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Does NYPD report to you infractions that they've had?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Or how are you coordinating with the other agencies to enforce infractions?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: So we do coordinate with the police department and the parks department for on-street enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: That includes providing them with regular updates about the licensed actors in the industry.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: But they don't report to you.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: They get a number of petty cab complaints or actions that they take.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: They don't hand that information over to you.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We don't have the outcomes necessarily from those adjudications.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So there could be infractions that are being reported, but DCWP doesn't know what they are, so you can't do it.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: You don't receive that information.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: You can't enforce around bad actors.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So I think like...

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: That's one of the reasons that I think perhaps another agency is better equipped to keep this, you know, to really enforce among

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: bad actors that has that kind of enforcement ability on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Because I think...

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: You know, in my district, you know, we do, we get complaints all the time about particularly a lot of noise, like traffic infractions, where other agencies are being called.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: But, you know, that's not getting back to your agency that issues the, you know, the permits for this.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Do you have, is there, if it were to remain at DCWP, how could you, you know, fill that gap?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: What would be, like, could, how could we fix that?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Well, I think we want to continue building our ties with the community stakeholders to ensure that they understand the obligations they have.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Additionally, I think we want to work with PD in particular to facilitate a lot of the enforcement that's required for the unlicensed activity.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I actually don't think necessarily it's the license actors that are causing the problems in this industry.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I like, and we work closely with these folks too.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I know that they want to be compliant.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: They're doing as much as they can to follow the rules.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think it's really the unlicensed actors that are causing the biggest issues.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And I think we need to figure out some solutions for how we can bring better enforcement efforts against those.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks Ortiz for specific suggestions to improve the industry, including electric, timing, and pricing issues. Ortiz says meters and rates could improve pricing clarity and level the playing field for consumers and businesses.
chapters.title: Brewer questions DCWP on improving the pedicab industry

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: All right, thank you, Councilmember Wilson.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Now we're going to go to Councilmember Brewer and then Councilmember Hanks.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Danielle, you need to fill out a form.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Whoever's here from Midtown, I can see you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You need to fill out a form.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: A couple questions for Carlos, the great Carlos Diaz.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What if you, I mean, in some cases you stated this.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: PD can decide, somebody else can decide.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How do you suggest other than, you know, because it's not TLC yet.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I hope it is.
