utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How do you suggest this industry be improved?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What would be some specific suggestions that you would make?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I mean, we've got electric issues, we've got timing issues, we've got...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: All the topics that I think were covered in some of this legislation.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What would you do specifically to improve this industry?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think, and I can speak from my own personal experience as well, I think the pricing- You take a pedicab too?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I've taken a pedicab.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Oh, good.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And the pricing definitely impacted me.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And I think that some of the legislation, for example, today related to meters and rates, I think could be a vast improvement on the industry as well.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: So I think it's just the consumer side of things.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: It ensures clarity.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: It ensures that we're all operating on the same level playing field.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think that would be a big help to the industry.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: When you say level playing field, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I mean, I liked, I mean, what do I mean?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I mean that it's good for a consumer and a business to have the same understanding of what the outcome of a transaction is going to be.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And a meter could facilitate that or rates could facilitate that.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think it's also important from business to business as well, that they have a mutual understanding of what's going to happen when a transaction with a consumer occurs.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: So that's what I would like to elaborate on, leveling the playing field.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks how one gets a pedicab license and how many have been suspended. Ortiz explains the annual spring lottery for registration plates, annual compliance checks, and plate removal for failed inspections.
chapters.title: Brewer questions DCWP on pedicab license lottery and suspensions

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I mean, 330 have a license, 1,200 operating.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I think that's probably correct.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How does one go about getting a license?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And I think, I don't know if you answered this, but how many have been suspended?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: If any, recently.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: There's an annual lottery that the agency conducts over the springtime to issue registration plates to licensed pedicab businesses.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And once you're selected for a lottery, you can get the registration plate.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think in the last lottery,

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We were able to get up to 330 total registered vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: When you become a licensee, we do compliance checks on your vehicle to ensure that the cab condition is accurate, the signage is accurate.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We do those annually.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: If a business fails that annual inspection, we will take away the plate until there's a correction to that issue.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: But I think, you know, again...

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: There's a small subset of actors, or there's a small subset of the industry that are following the rules.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: That's 330 folks.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: But clearly, for all of us who've been in these spaces, we know that there's more pedicabs operating out there.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks whether pedicab businesses must carry insurance and how it works. Ortiz says the administrative code requires insurance, up to six companies offer it, but costs have risen and made licensing difficult.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about pedicab insurance requirements and costs

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: My most recent pedicab driver was, he was Russian, and I was on my way to the chess championship, and he joined me.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You never know what's next.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In terms of insurance, I guess that's the same issue.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Are they supposed to have insurance?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And how does that work in terms of obviously being expensive?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I know there are very few companies that provide it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How does the insurance work?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: If at all.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: So the administrative code requires these businesses to carry insurance.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And my understanding is there's up to six companies currently offering the industry insurance.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: But the costs have been going up in recent years, and that has also been difficult for the business actors to be able to get their license.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: In terms of determining how an insurance policy, if it's complying with the ad code, we work with the law department to review those policies.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks how many cases go to OATH and what happens. Ortiz says most NYPD summonses do not go to OATH, and Brewer says many fail because officers' handwritten summonses are unreadable, leading judges to dismiss them.
chapters.title: Brewer questions DCWP on OATH cases and summons dismissals

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And then how does, do you talk to Oath about those cases that are brought to Oath?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How many cases do you know in what time period are brought to Oath and what happens there?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you have any sense of that effort?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: My understanding is the majority of the summonses that PD issues are not to oath.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: They issue principally C summonses or B summonses with oath, but there are some that do go to oath, so we're working to build ties with oath for greater information transmission.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And it helps that our former commissioners are there as well, so we'll be reaching out to them to see if we can formalize that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Oh, no, so the ones that PD deals with, they deal with them themselves.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Those are the ones that the chair was asking about that often don't go very far.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The reason they don't go very far is the cops, with all due respect, don't know how to write.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And so it's hard to read, and then the judge says, sorry, can't read it, goodbye, because I go to the court and I listen, and that's what happens.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So that's a whole other topic about writing versus putting it on some kind of a digital format.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But so your cases don't go to oath.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Your cases do or do not go to oath.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I thought they did.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Our cases would go to oath.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: But the on-street enforcement is handled by PD.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Brewer says pedicabs are supposed to be non-electric but almost all appear electric. Ortiz confirms motorized pedicabs are illegal and can be summonsed or confiscated, and Brewer says she personally thinks electric assist makes sense.
chapters.title: Brewer asks how DCWP handles electric pedicabs

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The other question I have is the...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Electric bike versus regular bike.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Now, my understanding is pedicabs are supposed to be regular bike and not electric.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They are mostly, I think, almost 100% electric.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How do you handle that?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I personally feel they should be electric because it's hard to pedal and you want to get people where you're going.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So how do you handle that issue?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: So you're correct that pedicabs are...

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: are not allowed to be motorized right now.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And it is grounds for the police to issue a summons or to confiscate a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Let me, and I want to get back to another question you asked earlier, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: So let me throw to my colleague to describe the revocations we've done.

chapters.summary: Haley Radiker says DCWP typically moves to revoke licenses during renewal. Since 2022, DCWP revoked about 90 pedicab licenses, including 21 driver licenses and 68 business licenses.
chapters.title: Radiker reports 90 pedicab license revocations since 2022

utterances.speaker: Haley Radiker
utterances.text: Yeah, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Haley Radiker
utterances.text: So just on our revocations, we typically will move to revoke licenses during the renewal period.

utterances.speaker: Haley Radiker
utterances.text: So since 2022, we have revoked about 90 licenses for pedicabs.

utterances.speaker: Haley Radiker
utterances.text: 21 of those were for drivers and 68 were for businesses.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'll do other questions second round.

chapters.summary: Council Member Kamillah Hanks asks whether registered pedicabs are retrofitting motors or whether unregistered devices dominate. Ortiz says it is hard to know but unlicensed actors likely ignore rules, and Hanks asks where enforcement and policy can meet given resource limits.
chapters.title: Hanks questions DCWP on electric-assist pedicabs and enforcement resources

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I'm going to turn it over to Councilmember Hanks and then Councilmember Maloney.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: My line of questioning is also surrounding around the motorized, the electric motor allowing on pedicabs with Intro 1063.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: The council investigation found that the vast majority of pedicabs have motors despite being prohibited.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Do you think that registered pedicabs are retrofitting their vehicles with pedal assist, or are these primarily unregistered devices?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think it's hard to say.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I would think that there's 330 registered pedicab vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think we talked earlier about reporting showing there's much more unlicensed vehicles out there.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I would tend to think that it's the unlicensed actors that are not following the rules of the road, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: But certainly our annual compliance checks are where we're viewing for the motors not being present.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: And where do you see this going with so many unregistered vehicles?

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: NYPD has their own opinion.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: We're definitely trying to come up with legislation and policy that will keep New Yorkers safe.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: But it seems like this is one of those spaces where we may not have the...

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: The resources, I think when you testified, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Goldapper, that some of this legislation is extremely costly to implement.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So if you can kind of talk about where do you think this is going as far as enforcement and policy and where the council and the administration can kind of meet in the middle.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I can start on that and throw it over to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: You know, I think to echo Councilmember Brewer's statement at the top, I think this hearing is long overdue.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: There are solutions that we could have that we can agree on already on pricing, for example, that I think would help improve the industry.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And I think there's more work needs to be done.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: DCP, candidly, I think we want to make sure we're creating deeper ties with the sister agencies that are conducting the on-street enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Because ultimately, we do want to have an industry that is successful for not just tourists, but New Yorkers in the future as well.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: To the second part of your question, let me throw it to my colleague, Deputy Commissioner Goldapper.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: So any increase in scope will certainly require additional resources.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Refer, you know, as with respect to updating equipment and technologies,

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: staffing for enforcement and prosecution, and the level of engagement needed to actually understand the issues at hand.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: We do not, TLC does not know the pedicab industry.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: We are familiar with the for-hire vehicle and taxi cab industry, and we are more than willing to work as partners with DCWP and other sister agencies as well as the council

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: to come up and assist with the approach.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: There are a number of things that I don't, excuse me, I don't believe it could just be as simple as a copy and paste of how we regulate taxis.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: It's a different industry.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: But we are more than happy to share the things that we do within licensing, inspections, enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: And the subject matter experts can then review these things to determine what may be applicable or appropriate.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: in the pedicab industry.

chapters.summary: Hanks asks whether DCWP receives consumer complaints about electric-assist pedicabs. Ortiz says those complaints go to NYPD, and he defers to DOT and NYPD on safety, noting concerns about identifying vehicles and speed but also workers' need for assistance.
chapters.title: Hanks asks DCWP about electric-assist complaints and safety

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: I think that we'll have to dig into that offline.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: But back to a question for you.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Do you receive a lot of consumer complaints about pedicabs with electric assist?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: The agency does not receive those complaints.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I believe they would go directly to the police department.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So maybe we should have public safety here as well.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Do you think it's appropriate for pedicabs to use electric pedal assist?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: No, I think I'm speaking with my colleagues at DOT and NYPD, who I think we would defer to on kind of the street safety aspects of this policy.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I know DOT has concerns about allowing more electric vehicles on the streets if enforcement is still an issue.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I know PD has a concern with identifying vehicles, make sure they're going the right speed.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: But that said, we also have a lot of businesses and workers that are trying to make a living out there, and the vehicles would help them do that.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: So I think there's a balance there where we should hear both sides of that.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: But I could see how it's difficult to move into that space until we have greater compliance happening in the industry overall.

chapters.summary: Council Member Virginia Maloney asks for geographic data on pedicab complaints and summonses. Ortiz says NYPD holds that data and DCWP can request it, and says pedicabs operate mainly in Central Park and the theater district.
chapters.title: Maloney asks for geographic breakdown of pedicab complaints and enforcement

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Hanks.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And I'm going to hand it over to Councilmember Maloney.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And then after Councilmember Maloney, we'll go to Councilmember Shulman.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Epstein.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And thank you for your testimony and for being here.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I represent the east side of Manhattan and parts of Midtown.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And I don't think it's a coincidence we've got, of the questions, four out of five coming from folks who represent

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Do you have data on the geographic breakdown?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I know we were digging into a lot of the numbers around the number of pedicabs, the number of pedicabs that are unlicensed, as well as the complaints and summonses by geographic

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: area or by borough.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We do not have that data broken down by, it's with the police department.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: But we can request the police department to provide us the geographic breakdown for you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: That would be great.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And what about where the vehicles operate right now?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: My understanding is predominantly they're operating in Central Park in the theater district.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And then what about the enforcement resources?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Are they appropriately allocated by geographic area where we're seeing the vast majority of the pedicab activity?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Well, the enforcement resources, you know, it's...

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: The police department and the parks department conduct the on-street enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I know they have established commands in Central Park and parts of Midtown, and that they'll strategically deploy more folks to help with enforcement when there are operations happening or there's peak seasons happening.

chapters.summary: Maloney notes NYPD, DOT, and Parks are not at the table and says a solution is needed now. She asks how long it would take TLC to build capacity if given pedicab oversight, and Goldapper says it is difficult to estimate and would require OMB analysis.
chapters.title: Maloney asks TLC how long transition would take

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I think just echoing some of the comments from earlier, it seems that two of the major, three of the major enforcement agencies are not at the table.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So NYPD, DOT, Parks, with DCWP only covering a small piece of the pie of the complaints that we're hearing on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: There's the tourist issues with scams and overcharging, but the vast majority are safety issues, speeding,

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: noise complaints, and then standing in no standing zones and cluttering the streets, which is what is the motivation behind the bill.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: is in this package to create buffer zones of about 50 feet or so from these major tourist destinations.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: One of the things we're spending a lot of time talking about is TLC versus DCWP, better coordination with NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: One of the concerns I have is we need a solution now.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: How long would it take if we were to

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: shift this responsibility over to TLC to build up that capacity to enforce.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: It's actually very difficult to estimate.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: There are a number of, I guess, new bills related to the industry floating around, whether it's manual pedal versus e-bike.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: So we would need to sort of have a better understanding of the full responsibilities required in order to do that.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: But we could work with OMB for a timeline and estimation of the resources needed.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Because we would still have to ensure that the for-hire vehicle industry needs are met as well.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: We have over 180,000 licensed drivers across the city of New York.

chapters.summary: Ortiz clarifies DOT is not an on-street enforcement agency. Maloney asks about technology to track pedicab locations and whether BIDs could get enforcement powers; Ortiz says BIDs are good partners and DCWP is working on automated interagency reporting.
chapters.title: Maloney asks about technology and expanding BID enforcement powers

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Can I also just clarify something I think I was imprecise about?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: NYPD and the Parks Department are the primary enforcement agencies on the street.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: The DOT is not involved in the enforcement side of that picture.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: One other, I want to introduce two solutions, creative solutions to try to get to enforcement, which it sounds like we all agree is one of the biggest issues.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Are there technologies that are being explored to ensure that pedicabs are operating where they're supposed to, are not standing?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And then bids often have jurisdiction or are supporting many of the areas where pedicabs are operating.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Is there a way that the enforcement powers could be expanded to bids?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Or any other creative solutions you have to help us get to the enforcement issue as fast as possible.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Yeah, I would say the bids have been great partners to us on this issue.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I would certainly be interested in looking into more of how we can support one another in terms of any enforcement activities.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: The first part of your question, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Technologies that could be explored or any other ideas for how to get to enforcement, which it sounds like we all agree is the biggest challenge here.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Yeah, so we are looking to create greater connections via automated reports between agencies so that we can get that information on a regular basis and move quicker.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: That work is ongoing.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Maloney.

chapters.summary: Council Member Lynn Schulman asks whether noise complaints about pedicabs can be filed with DCWP. Ortiz says 311 noise complaints go to NYPD or DEP, and Schulman says the city needs a protocol; DCWP does not have noise complaint data and will request it.
chapters.title: Schulman asks about noise complaints and penalties

utterances.text: Now over to Councilmember Schultz.

utterances.text: Can a complainant file a noise-related complaint about a pedicab business or driver to DCWP?

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Yeah, it's not you, Lynn.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I believe if somebody filed the 311 complaint about noise, it would go to the police department or go to DEP.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: You know, maybe there's, I mean, the legislation's not on the table here, but maybe it's a question of with, I have a bill in to 311 complaints to go to where the actual issue is.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: the agency, so just FYI there.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: But I think in the issue of consumer complaining about noise happening in the street, I think from our perspective, we want to try to address it in real time as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Or bring the enforcement agent that can bring the summons against that activity.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And that's why it goes to PD or to DEP.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Although I know that sometimes...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And Stan, it's just, they're all over the place, so we don't have exactly, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So we need to have some kind of protocol.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: All right, in relation to that question, if so, in the past year, how many noise-related complaints have been filed against pedicure drivers?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Do you have an idea of that or you don't?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We don't have that.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: You don't.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Can you get that?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Yes, Councilman.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: How many of those complaints resulted in penalties imposed on the pedicab driver or the pedicab business?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Does that eventually?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: For noise complaints, we would have to pull that information from the other agencies.

chapters.summary: Schulman asks about the content of overcharging complaints. Ortiz says they are case-by-case but mostly involve overcharging rather than posted-price violations, and DCWP has received 335 overcharging complaints since 2022.
chapters.title: Schulman asks for details on overcharging complaints

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So I'm going to go on to different questions.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Apologies, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: You know.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: How many, we know that overcharging is the most frequent pedicab complaint to 311 and DCWP.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: That's you, right, Carlos?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Can you share more details about the content of these complaints?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: For example, are they related to exorbitant prices or alleging that pedicab drivers are charging consumers more than the posted price?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think it's case by case.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: It could be a mix.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I would say when I've looked through the complaints and the coding, the vast majority seem to be more about overcharging and less about the advertising per se.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: So I would say, yeah, since 2022, 335 complaints related to overcharging.

chapters.summary: Schulman asks about per-minute rates indexed to inflation and scannable codes. Ortiz says pricing clarity and meters could help, but fixed rates need more discussion, and DCWP is evaluating the cost of scannable registration plates.
chapters.title: Schulman questions DCWP on fixed rates and scannable registration codes

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Does the administration have any concerns about setting a per-minute rate for pedicabs that's indexed to inflation?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think, as I was mentioning earlier, pricing clarity is something that I think this industry could benefit from.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Fixed rates is, however, I think it's a big step, not just for the agency, but also for the businesses and for the workers.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: So I think I want to make sure that I have understanding of the implications on those businesses'ability to operate, the compliant businesses.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: On how fixed rates would impact them.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Certainly, meters is a conversation where we're ready to have.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think meters would be very beneficial.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Fixed rates, I think, is something that we still want to talk through with the council.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So related a little bit to what the chair asked before in terms of if you go somewhere else, another city, another country or whatever,

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: does the administration have any concerns with creating a scannable code that can be used to trace the pedicab registration number and the name of the pedicab business?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: That we are still evaluating for the cost on scannable registration.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: But we can, should this bill advance, we could provide those costs.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Because if you have scannable codes, then it would help somebody actually have scannable codes to how much is supposed to charge and all that kind of stuff.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: All of that, that somebody who's not from somewhere else can do that.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Yes, I understand the goals for the scannable codes.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think for us, we would like to share budgetary implications for creating that scannable code for this smaller industry that we license.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: But not to say that we're...

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: No, no, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I was going to say, not to say that we're not open to having a discussion about this.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: It's just that we want to make sure we're sharing the full context of the implications of legislation.

chapters.summary: Schulman says the bills are practical and the city must find solutions despite resource issues across agencies. Ortiz agrees the problems need creative solutions and thanks the committee.
chapters.title: Schulman says bills are practical and agencies need solutions

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: A council investigation found that the vast majority of pedicabs have motor...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Oh, we did this already.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I think these bills are pretty...

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Pretty good in what they're asking for and I think that they're practical so we're gonna have we have to find some solutions because every agency is having resource issues

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: so and and I appreciate the work you do by the way so I just want to say that thank you council member and I and I

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And we need to come up with creative solutions for them as well.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz

chapters.summary: Epstein asks how often DCWP holds the pedicab license lottery and whether someone can apply outside it. Ortiz explains the annual spring lottery for vehicle plates, while driver licenses have no cap and can be applied for year-round.
chapters.title: Epstein questions DCWP on pedicab license lottery process

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Shulman.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to me for a few minutes, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So you mentioned the lottery.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: How often do you do a lottery for pedicab licensing?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: It's an annual lottery, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And if someone wants to apply outside the lottery, can they do that?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: My understanding is you can apply for the license and then the lottery throughout the year.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And then when you want to get the vehicle plates, you go through the lottery.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Okay, so today I leave here.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I'm like, you know, I really want to be a pedicab driver.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And so I can go fill out a form now, and that'll be valid until you decide if I'm eligible?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: For the driver license, you can apply for that.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: There's no cap on driver license, and you can become a driver.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: For pedicab businesses, you apply for the pedicab business license, and once you receive that license, you can submit for the lottery, even though the lottery happens once a year, to get a registered vehicle with the city.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And so the registered vehicle, that's how I can get it on the streets.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And when does that lottery happen?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: It's in the springtime.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: It's in April.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And so the pedicab businesses can only operate a registered vehicle.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And the only person who's allowed to be behind the handlebars of that vehicle is a pedicab driver.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You're saying if I want to get a new, I decide I have a career change and I want to get a vehicle, I have to wait until the springtime.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: to do that.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: But in the springtime, since you have over 800 available, but only 300 issued, who gets turned down then from those applications?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think it's a mixture of folks who might submit for the lottery, but then when they get awarded, they don't pick up the plate for whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And also people just not the full applicants to the lottery are not equal to the amount of registration plates available.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: How many applied last year for the lottery?

chapters.summary: Epstein asks how many businesses applied for the lottery and what percentage are turned down. Ortiz says 311 pedicab businesses have applied since 2024, and denials or revocations happen more at renewal or inspection than at the lottery stage.
chapters.title: Epstein asks how many apply for pedicab lottery and who is denied

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Since 2024, we've had 311 pedicab businesses apply for the lottery.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Each year or just they get renewal every year?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Renewals as well.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So what percentage of people get turned down who apply?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I'm not sure if we're turning down people at the lottery stage.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: It's more once you're a pedicab business and you apply for the lottery, you can get the plate.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We do a qualifying inspection.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: That's the annual inspection to ensure that the vehicle is compliant.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: If you've received a plate and we inspect you and your vehicle is not compliant, we would take that plate back and you're not allowed to operate that vehicle.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So assuming someone's got a vehicle and a personal license, they can ride the vehicle and it's operational.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: What percentage of those people are, is there anyone who's just not, who's getting turned down, who's applying?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Or they all just, once they apply and have a licensed vehicle, they're going to be able to become a pedicab operator?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: No, we have been denying folks that renewal and revoking licenses.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I know you mentioned you revoked 90.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Approximately 90, yes.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: But those people then were able to get new licenses again?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Were those 90 were able to, in subsequent years, get a license back?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Typically, there's a cooling off period after you've lost the license, and I think it's like a year, and then you can come back and get another one.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So of those 90, how many of them are currently operating?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I don't have that information, Jay.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Could you get it for us?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: That's true.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks why about three-quarters of pedicab operators do not apply for licenses. Ortiz says unlicensed activity has grown, incentives are off, and compliant actors should speak to why unlicensed activity persists; insurance costs may also be a factor.
chapters.title: Epstein asks why most pedicab operators remain unlicensed

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And so why do you think the vast majority of people, three-quarters of the people who are operating in this industry, aren't even bothering to apply for a license either for themselves or for their vehicle then?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think over the past few years, noncompliance has been particularly centered around unlicensed activity.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think when you have unlicensed activity and you're a licensed actor, the incentives are off.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And that's why I think we need to focus our force and education efforts back onto this industry as a city overall.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So you're saying people are making a cost-benefit analysis.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: They're saying the cost of applying for a license versus the risk of not applying for the license.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Three-quarters of people are not applying because in that risk analysis they're making, they're thinking it's more beneficial not to apply for the license because we'll have less oversight.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: You know, I think that could be part of it.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: But also, you know what I'd be really interested to hear on this question, too, is the compliant actors right now.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think they could really speak to us about why they're seeing in their industry unlicensed activity.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think there's an aspect of, I think it's always, it's inherently unfair for one business to be trying to comply as much as possible and other ones are not.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And we, as an enforcement mechanism, we want to ensure, generally as an administration, that the folks who are following the rules are rewarded, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We touched upon earlier insurance as well.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: My understanding from speaking to workers and businesses is that insurance costs are going up too.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I don't know if that's tied into the unlicensed activity as well.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think that's something to investigate further.

chapters.summary: Epstein worries that new regulations may hurt licensed operators while unlicensed ones ignore them. He asks what tools DCWP needs beyond ticketing, and Ortiz says the administration is open to discussing additional tools and wants Council action.
chapters.title: Epstein presses DCWP on incentives and enforcement tools

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So let me ask you.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Since this becomes a vastly unregulated industry by DCWP, since three-quarters of the people are licensed, so they're not regulated by you, passing further regulations is still going to then

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: potentially hurt the licensed people who are already being regulated by you because you can revoke their license.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And give more free reign to the unregulated people because they're like, well, not being regulated now, so the additional regulations won't hurt them.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: How do we incentivize it enough to get people in the fold to actually apply?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Well, I think let's take an example of the meters or rates, for example, or improved signage around rates.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: That is something that the police department would be able to enforce, whether that's an unlicensed or a licensed actor.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: So I think there's an ability to have new regulations here that we could use as further tools for enforcement of the issues that are arising.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think to what we've been discussing throughout the day is we need other solutions as well in terms of greater communication channels between agencies, greater communication channels with stakeholders.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: These things we also have to incorporate.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I'm just worried that the tool we have in our tool belt, which is ticketing, seems like not a really strong enforcement mechanism here to force people into a legal system.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And I'm wondering what advice...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: As the overseeing agency would have to craft other solutions besides just having NYPD continue to take it.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: 90% of those tickets aren't enforced.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Like, what other tools do you think you need to have?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We're talking about pricing.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You know, obviously, that's a– but that's just– people don't list the prices.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: It's just more tickets.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Like, I think we need other tools here to be able to push people into a regulatory scheme.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think we're open to having that conversation about what additional tools the administration can have for this industry.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And you just haven't come up with tools yet that you...

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Well, we've been working with folks in this room to try and address the situation for years, and we want to keep working at that.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: There's tools that ideally the council can give us today, and we'd be very excited for that.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: But it doesn't mean the conversation stops there.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks whether TLC's peace officers could enforce pedicab laws if given more funding. Goldapper says TLC does targeted enforcement, not patrols, and is not responsible for quality-of-life complaints like noise; he notes TLC's special patrolman status and pending peace-officer legislation.
chapters.title: Brewer asks TLC whether peace officers could enforce pedicab laws

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I know Councilmember Brewer has additional questions, so I want to hand it over to her.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Just a couple because I want to hear from people in the room.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: From the Taxi and Limousine Commission, you have peace officers, right?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So they could, in fact, do pedicabs.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Obviously, funding is an issue.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And I want to thank your commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We had a great conversation, and I appreciate her input.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But can you, I mean, TLC really has the authority already in some sense with peace officers to do the enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you believe that?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: If you had more money, it would be nice.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: I'll never say no to more resources.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Well, the chair said he was going to get you some more.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: He's good for it, I know.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: One thing I want to sort of point out, because I might not have been clear when I...

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: discussed what we do.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: We do not, when we target on license for higher activity, we are not patrolling across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You'd only have one borough.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: I'm still responsible for the $180,000.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: I'm the same with Pedicab.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You only have one borough.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: So we're not patrolling.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: These are targeted enforcement operations.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: And I know some of the issues that arose.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: You know, I'm hearing quality of life issues.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: We're not here to look to duplicate those quality of life enforcement that's handled by NYPD, sanitation, DEP.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: We specifically target unlicensed for hire operations.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: So when the idea of a quick response to say a noise complaint.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: We may not be there.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: In fact, because of the geographical constraints of the city for us and how large it is, we'll likely not be there.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: So the idea that someone makes a complaint for noise and

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: We don't respond.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: I hope I'm making that clear.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: It is targeted enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: And the other aspect is, you know, unlicensed for hire activity is in all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Any sort of diversion of resources is really going to be pulling resources from the outer boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: No, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But I'm just saying peace officers could, in fact, in the description, operate within the confines of what you do now.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It could be applied to pedicabs without getting into some of the other agencies and what they do.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: You know, I'm not actually entirely sure.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I think that's true, but I won't say anything more.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: Our status is through the Special Patrolman Program.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: We currently have a bill out there being considered to give us peace officer status without the Special Patrolman designation through NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Ira Goldapper
utterances.text: And that's, so I don't want to give you incorrect information.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But it's part of the ongoing discussion.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks how many people it would take to license pedicabs. Ortiz says DCWP has no dedicated pedicab unit and the work is absorbed into everyday tasks, estimating about two to three full-time employees.
chapters.title: Brewer asks DCWP how many staff would be needed for pedicab licensing

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: One more question for consumer.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How many people would it take, do you think, to license pedicabs?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Obviously, there are different agencies.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's complicated.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But what do you think would be a good?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Number.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Currently, we don't have a dedicated pedicab unit for licensing and reviews of licenses by our general counsel.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: It's work that's incorporated into the everyday tasks.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I would say full FTE, full-time employee, it's probably approximately two to three.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks whether DCWP has street enforcement staff for illegal tobacco or other violations. Ortiz says those inspectors focus on brick-and-mortar inspections because public-space enforcement is dangerous; DCWP inspectors have been assaulted and lack police powers.
chapters.title: Epstein questions DCWP on street enforcement and inspector safety

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And thank you, Councilmember Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Just a couple of last questions, and I'll let you all go.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So DCWP does have some people who do enforcement out on the street.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So if there's someone selling illegal, I don't know, I don't know, if you go to someone selling illegal cigarettes, Ben, but there are a lot of...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: They're not licensed for tobacco or they're licensed for tobacco and they're selling something else.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You have people who go out and do that enforcement, correct?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Can I elaborate a little bit more, though?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Those folks are focused on brick-and-mortar inspections.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And why?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Why are they focused on brick-and-mortar?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think, you know, speaking from my experience over the past 10 years, there are inherent challenges that we, our inspectors, face when conducting enforcement in public spaces.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I'm speaking from experience of street vending enforcement, for example, ticket seller enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Our folks are not police officers or officers in any kind of way.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: They don't have badges.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: They don't have the ability to detain people.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: In fact, we've actually had cases where our inspectors engaging in this type of

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: of enforcement in public spaces have been assaulted or threatened.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Even in the context of, you know, an unlicensed smoke shop, and we've shared this with the council previously, we have had inspectors who had doors closed on their hands or shutters brought down on their feet.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: It's really challenging for us then to try to expand that out into on-street enforcement of moving vehicles or

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: are ambulance actors.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Well, you could do enforcement in collaboration with another enforcement agency.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You could do the pedicab enforcement along with NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You could have staff on site.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You could both issue violations through DCWP and through NYPD, right?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We have done that in the past.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think, you know, without disparaging at all my colleagues in enforcement work who do amazing work, there is a certain redundancy and liability there.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: You know, in the context of that inspector who was assaulted during a ticket selling operation, he was with a police officer and it just created kind of another exposure.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: For an assault.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: So I think that's why we try to, as much as possible, leverage our expertise on the licensing and broader investigation scale, while PD's footprint on the on-street presence.

chapters.summary: Epstein says an unlicensed alcohol seller would be shut down easily, but unlicensed pedicabs seem harder to stop. He asks why enforcement is so difficult and what additional tools DCWP would need for on-street enforcement.
chapters.title: Epstein compares unlicensed pedicabs to unlicensed alcohol sales

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, I hear you.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And I'm just having a hard time figuring out, like, if we are having a problem of, like, three-quarters of this industry is illegal, and we all acknowledge it's a problem, and we acknowledge that we need to do better enforcement to fix the problem.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And we do have existing...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: tools.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You know, obviously we want to give you more tools.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: But it's, you know, it's like if someone's, you know, if I tomorrow wanted to go and start selling alcohol at a store around the corner from my house, I don't have a license to do it.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I would just get shut down.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: It would be easy to shut me down and the state liquor authority and everyone else would be like, you can't do that.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: But I don't know why it seems like when we see unlicensed activity, they're basically taking advantage of tourists and sometimes New Yorkers, why this seems like it's a harder effort.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And so that's what I'm struggling with here.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think for us, you know, I think the on-street enforcement,

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: creates a challenge for us with the tools that we have available.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So what tools would you want to have available if you were going to do on-screen enforcement then?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: What additional tool would be helpful?

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I don't know if pushing the agency into on-screen enforcement is the right approach for this work, given the fact that we are not, you know, our inspectors are not equipped for that.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I think the strength of this agency, as we've showcased over the past year, if not more, is our ability to bring enforcement actions through investigations against larger players in the industry.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I know in the context of ticket sellers...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: But, Carlos, why stay involved in this industry at all, then?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: If, like, it's not leaning into your strengths...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Why do we just not, you know, you can still license and let enforcement happen in other places because it doesn't seem like NYPD has the tools.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: They're struggling.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Why are we not thinking creatively about a better way to do enforcement here?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And I think that's what I think Councilmember Brewer and we're trying to get at here.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: It's like we have a problem that we should be able to fix here.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And, you know, I think we're dancing around that a bit.

chapters.summary: Ortiz says DCWP wants to be part of the conversation and recognizes the industry's problems. He says the hearing is not the end of the discussion but part of setting larger solution goals.
chapters.title: Ortiz says hearing is part of larger solution conversation

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: I would say coming to this hearing today, we want to be a part of this conversation as an administration.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: We recognize that there are issues with this industry, issues with the way that things are set up.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: And this is not, I think, a period on what's the conversation.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: This is a part of, I think, a larger solution goal setting we have to set.

chapters.summary: Epstein thanks the agency panel and dismisses it. He reminds the public that this is a formal proceeding, asks for decorum, and instructs anyone wishing to testify to sign up with the sergeant and submit transcripts within 72 hours.
chapters.title: Epstein dismisses agency panel and instructs public witnesses

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I appreciate all your time.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And unless there's any more questions from our colleagues, this panel is dismissed.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: If people in the public are here to testify, they should be signing up with the sergeant for testimony.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I remember the public that this is a formal government proceeding.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Decorum shall be reserved at all times.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Please be silent and don't approach the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: There's no video recording or photography allowed at the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Members of the public may not present audio video recordings at testimony, but they can submit transcripts and such stuff to the sergeant at arms later.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Again, please, if you want to testify, sign up to testify and you know the hearing topics.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: testimony, you can do that and submit that to the Sergeant at Arms or submit that within 72 hours.

chapters.summary: Danielle Mendez, who oversees the Midtown Community Justice Center, says the bills reflect roundtable recommendations for comprehensive reform. She says the current system does not incentivize licensing or registration, lets anyone print DCWP signage, and criminalizes a primarily immigrant workforce while failing to address overcharging.
chapters.title: Danielle Mendez testifies on pedicab criminal summonses and reform

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And we now have our first panel, which is Danielle.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Minkless, Minkless, Kenneth Winter, and McCann Camara.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We just, we have our first panel.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: If you want to just start and we can get to the other panelists after.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Well, before we start, we're also joined by Council Member Banks.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you for joining us.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: I'm Danielle Mendez.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: I oversee the Midtown Community Justice Center where the pedicab criminal summonses are heard.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Epstein and members of the committee for hearing this package of bills that reflect the recommendations surfaced at the roundtable we held late last year.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: Those recommendations guided the development of Intros 77, 673, 1026, 1063, 992, and 993.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: Together, these bills include the components of comprehensive reform required to fix this dysfunctional industry.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: The current status quo does not incentivize drivers to get licensed.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: It does not incentivize vehicle owners to register their vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: Vehicles can't easily be connected to their owners.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: It does not allow consumers to easily identify legitimate pedicabs on the street or to know how much a ride will cost.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: The signage DCWP currently provides for registered cabs is printed off a computer.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: Anybody could make one.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: It simultaneously criminalizes a primarily immigrant workforce by relying on law enforcement to respond to infractions in what should be a professional industry.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: There's been a lot of discussion today and around this issue in general around overcharging consumers and ripping off tourists.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: And I just want to be really clear that this is not what we're seeing in court.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: Those issues are not being handled at all.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: In most cases, these kinds of infractions would constitute misdemeanor arrest, not summonses, and we're not seeing those.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: The cases coming into court are most frequently, over the last three months, these are the most frequent summonses.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: Pedicabs without headlights, pedicabs without battery-operated taillight, without registration, no pedicab driver license, and operating in a bicycle lane.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: The things that people really care about are not being addressed in court and are largely not being addressed at all.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: There's something wrong with an industry if every worker who operates within it ends up in criminal court at some point.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: And yet none of the issues people care about are actually being addressed.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: We expect that shifting oversight of pedicabs from DCWP to TLC will bring about the licensing and enforcement changes required for a healthy industry, but only if additional resources are provided to that agency to do it the right way.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: This hearing represents a chance for the council to pass public policy solutions that have the full support of almost all parties who care about this issue.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: We were able to confirm that when we had our roundtable and wrote our report.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: I thank you very much for your consideration.

chapters.summary: Makan Camara, president of the New York Pedicab Alliance, says honest drivers are judged by cheaters and that enforcement is the top priority. He supports electric pedal assist, transparent pricing, affordable meters, fixed rates reflecting costs, rest spaces, and relief from insurance costs.
chapters.title: Makan Camara of New York Pedicab Alliance calls for enforcement and electric assist

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Okay, go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Chair and members of the committee, my name is Makan Kamara, president of the New York Pedicure Alliance, known as the NIPA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Two years ago, we came together because we were afraid of losing the work that feeds our family.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Honest drivers were being judged by the actions of people which cheated passengers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: We could not stand by and let those people destroy everything we had worked for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: That is why we created NIPA in 2024.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: We are pedicure drivers and owners who spend our days on the streets, welcoming visitors and showing them the city we love.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: When we finish a long day of pedaling, we go home as parents, spouses, and people whose families depend on us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: For us, protecting this industry means protecting our ability to put food on the table and pay the rent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Our members gave from their earnings to keep this effort going.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Our committee gave their time, their money, and their energy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Even when people doubted us, they kept showing up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Today, I carry their hopes into this room.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: We want our passengers to be safe, and we want honest drivers to be able to keep working with dignity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Our number one priority is enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: When a passenger is cheated, that person suffers, and every honest driver lost trust.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: We're committed to work with city officials to protect passengers, stop scams, and hold dishonest operators accountable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Electricity assistance matters deeply to us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: We're not asking to go faster.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: asking for help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Cutting up to three people and pedaling for hours puts tremendous strength on our bodies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: In 2026, safe pedal assistance should not be a privilege.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: It should be a right for people doing this demanding work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: We support clear safety standards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Please recognize the human being

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: the human being behind the pedals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: We support transparent pricing, accessible training and identification that helps passengers recognize licensed operators.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Meter must be affordable and reliable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Fixed rate must reflect an operating cost.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Drivers also need lawful places to rest and pick up passengers and meaningful relief from insurance costs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Please reconcile these proposals so safe electoral assistance, our independent status, and the removal of imprisonment are preserved under whichever agency regulates us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: This decision will affect whether parents can keep working and family can pay their bills.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: We want reform that protects passengers and give honest drivers a fairer future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Give working drivers a meaningful role in shaping these rules.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: NAIPA is ready to do its part.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Please work with us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Makana.

chapters.summary: Kenneth Winter, a 23-year industry veteran and licensed tour guide, says he developed neuropathy and mobility issues after 15 years without electric assist. He is now a single father and needs electric assist to keep working, and he hopes the hearing brings positive change.
chapters.title: Kenneth Winter describes 23 years in pedicab industry and need for electric assist

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carlos Ortiz
