utterances.text: Go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: First time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: My name is Kenneth Winter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: I am a 23-year veteran of the industry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: I've been working this job for a very long time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: I will admit that I do use an electric assist and that I did the first 15 years of my profession.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: I am also a licensed tour guide, by the way, but I did the first 15 years of my profession without one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: This has led to me developing a neuropathy in my legs and some mobility issues, which also led to venous insufficiency, which makes it a little more difficult for me to operate my vehicle.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: But I am now a single father as of 2020.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: Due to the pandemic, which caused a lot of problems, a lot of the enforcement fell away, and it's made the industry more difficult to operate in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: But I need the electric assist because I need to be able to keep working.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: I can't be idealistic anymore like I used to be, and it's too late for me to make really a change in career.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: Anyway, this is what I am and what I do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: I'm an ambassador for the city of New York, and I basically...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: Engage in teaching and also, I guess, hosting visitors to the city of New York and do my very best to show New York City in its best light.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: All I can do is hope that these hearings will bring a positivity, a positive change to the industry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: Some of the issues that I've heard so far, I'm sure can be addressed and I'm sure I speak for our organization when I say that we're very open and willing

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: to be able to participate with all of the agencies involved in order to try to help them to reach our goals, which is better this industry and make it a

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: part of the actual network of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: transportation in the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks why most in the industry are unlicensed. Winter says enforcement fell away during the pandemic, insurance costs rose from about $600 to $5,000–$6,000 per unit, and drivers saw no consequences for operating without licenses.
chapters.title: Epstein asks public panel why most pedicab operators are unlicensed

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So let me ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Why do you think the vast majority of people in this industry are unlicensed?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And like, is there just a disincentive to get licensed?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: If anyone can answer.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Sorry, I apologize.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: I just want to make sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: So you hit it on the nail earlier that there's no incentive for anyone to really

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: tried to, when the pandemic happened, a lot of the enforcement fell away.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: And so it made it more, people were encouraged by the fact that there was no enforcement to continue operating without a license and without insurance and without a lot of these other things that they're required to have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: So on top of that,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: I sort of disagree with one of these CWP representatives about there being six insurance companies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: There's actually about two, three maximum.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: One of them has just started opening up to us, but the price of that insurance is exorbitant, $5,000 or higher.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: Per unit for a single year, which that's gone up about 90%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: Well, actually, 900% actually, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: Yeah, it's about 10 times more than what it used to be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: And so it's made it much more difficult for legal operators to be able to obtain this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: But the fact that there was no enforcement also encouraged them to not bother to get those licenses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: I had a driver come up to me and told me that he stopped getting the license and the insurance about three years ago because he saw that there was no consequence for it, so what's the point?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So people on license, even if they're getting tickets, they're meaningless, basically?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: Well, I think that there might be a disconnect sometimes between agencies in which one agency enforces a certain part and maybe the other agency doesn't really get that information in time.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So you're saying NYP?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: PD doesn't do that kind of ticketing that's referenced.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: They do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: It's just kind of a little disparate sometimes in the way they do it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: And I think one of the problems is they're not coordinating things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: As you just see from the DCWP, all the questions you're asking them, pretty much our NYPD, they don't have, for the most part, they don't have the answer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Because one of the first problems we just kind of, when we created NYPA, is the coordinating.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: They're not coordinating.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: You ask NYPD, they say go to DCWP.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: You go to them, they say go to NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: And that's for two years now, we don't have an answer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: And to go back to just what Kenny said about insurance, about why this unlicensed thing is there now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Before the COVID, pretty much the insurance was $600 for one unit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: But now we're almost close to $6,000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: And we don't know why.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: We asked DCWP, no answer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: We asked anybody, no answer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: And now it keeps increasing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: You know, and I'm not defending driver or owners, but it could be one of the factors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Because before COVID, 100% everybody was pretty much, you know, everybody has a license.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: But then when you move from 600 to almost 6,000, that could be one of the problems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: You know, so, yeah.

chapters.summary: Danielle Mendez says consumers have no way to identify which pedicabs are licensed and safe. She says clearer plates, barcodes, and consumer education could help, but agency information-sharing failures prevent accountability.
chapters.title: Mendez says consumers cannot identify licensed pedicabs

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: I'd just like to add in addition that the consumer has no opportunity to help drive out the unlicensed drivers by identifying which cabs are safe to get in, right?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: There's really no way to identify.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: on the street.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: And that seems like an inexpensive fix to make it very, very clear which cabs are licensed by this city and which are not and make it hard for cabs that look illegitimate to get riders.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: In addition to right-sizing the insurance, of course.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So do you think with more information on the street or through DCWBP or on the cab itself, people and consumers will be able to make better informed choices?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Or is it if they're still going to be able to just...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: The unlicensed pedicabs still going to be able to just say, well, you know, come us, we're cheaper, or like they're still going to incentivize people doing this.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Like, I'm not sure what's driving people to get into a licensing scheme if they can just operate.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And potentially defraud consumers, or even if they don't defraud them, charge them the same price, there's no incentive in the structure we have right now to license people.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: I completely agree with you.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: I think this is a multi-pronged answer, which is why we put forth a report with a series of multi-part recommendations that tax us from different angles.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: But I do think that's one aspect of it.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: There could be a consumer education campaign around which pedicabs to get into, which not to get into, and to have plates that are legitimate looking and a barcode that actually...

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: actually associates the registration and the license of the person driving the cab.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: Right now, as Kenny and McCann shared, there's no information sharing between agencies, so there's no way to hold anybody accountable.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: And like I said, consumers are just sort of taking their chances.

chapters.summary: Winter says each agency does its job but lacks connectivity, so enforcement is canceled out. He describes a 'gold rush' where unlicensed drivers charge per-minute, per-person rates of $9–$25 and use lights and sound to distract customers.
chapters.title: Winter describes agency disconnect and per-minute rip-offs

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: Every agency that has participated in trying to do enforcement has done an excellent job within their own field.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: The problem is that because of that disconnect, sometimes the work of one agency is canceled out by another.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: And so because there is no real...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: Connectivity there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: Also, I should mention that a lot of the reason why a lot of these guys do this is because it's really the almighty dollar.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: It's become like the new gold rush when it comes to the pedicab industry because they tell other people to come down to New York City and do this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: 65 million visitors, 42 million to the park, plenty of people you can rip off.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: Some of the people that I've encountered on the street have been bragging about how much they make.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: They almost want to tell you how much they're making.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: The reason why is because they can do these 15, 20-minute rides and nail the customer and disappear into the mist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: These rip-offs don't really happen much in the park, although we've discovered there's a few bad actors in the park as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: But the reason why is because the park is structured, so it doesn't make sense for them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: us to charge on these per minute rates.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: So most of us, we charge flat fees.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: But the guys on the street, they're abusing the system, given that they can charge whatever they want.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: It's a per minute per ride thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: But no one's putting these signs on the sides of the bike.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: And when they are, they're very tiny, black on red, black on gray, very tiny little lettering.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: And they're deceptive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: Or they just simply pull out a rate card at the end of the ride.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: That's also part of the reason for the lights and sound.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: The lights and sound is to attract and then distract.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: They get you into the bike, looks like fun.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: You come to the end of the ride and all of a sudden it's per minute per person, $9 to $25 a minute per person.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: And this is part of the reason why I feel that a price cap might also help with that maximum rate that will allow the customer to eventually have consumer confidence again, knowing that they're not going to be charged more than this particular rate per ride.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks whether the panel supports a taxi-style meter with a base fare and per-minute charge. Makan Camara says the New York Pedicab Alliance supports price clarity and meters, and Central Park operators already quote flat fees.
chapters.title: Epstein asks panel about meter and price-cap support

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And so you guys support the idea of like a meter like a cab has where it would just say, you know, you get in and it's $5 for one to make it a number of $5 to get in.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: But every minute after there's an additional cost.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: You know, I want to speak for the NIPA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Yes, we do support like, you know, the price system that's going to, you know, kind of because we want clarity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: You know, as Kenny said, 80 percent or I said 90 percent of the people from NIPA are Central Park people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: We 100% we people know exactly how much they're gonna pay because we agree on things you know what they want to do because for people who are familiar with Central Park you know small loop you know the you know lower loop whatever so we we

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: tell them exactly how it's going to be, or food that are bad apples, you know, and that's why we created an iPad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: That's why we want to work with good people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: So, and just to go back to the previous question about why, you know, this problem license versus unlicensed thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: One of the things is people who don't have, for example, were not licensed, and they're not afraid of anything.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: For example,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: If, for example, the NYPD sees your bike with, you know, unlicensed bike and stuff like that, a couple of weeks, a couple of days, you get your bike back.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: So then, and they, because we know each other, you know, so people, they say, why would I bother to even do this while you guys are having license and you were doing the same thing?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: We all, so we want, what we want as a night part, you know, we just make sure if somebody's bike being seized, you know, with fake plate or whatever, and there should be some type of laws or rules

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: to make sure these people, either they have to come with, you know, the right plate or something, or unless, you know, because otherwise they're going to keep doing whatever they're doing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: If they're going to give their bike back in two weeks or three weeks, it will go nowhere.

chapters.summary: Winter describes being stopped on July 8, 2026, while carrying two pedicabs. He provided license, insurance, and inspection documents, but NYPD confiscated one pedicab for electric assist, costing him about 20 days of work and major hardship.
chapters.title: Winter recounts pedicab confiscation for electric assist

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: Just to give you one more example, July 8th of this year, I was finally targeted for the electric assist on my pedicabs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: I happened to have both pedicabs with me because I rented a bike out to a movie.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: I have a second pedicab that I never use.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: I only have it as a backup.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: And I rented it to the movie, and I happened to pick it up that day from the movie set, and I happened to have them both with me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: It's around 11 p.m.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: That night.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: I was having some pizza on 54th Street and 7th Avenue, and one of the units rolled up on me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: And despite, even though I was stopped earlier that day by a different unit, I basically, every time that it happens, I gladly provide my license, provide my insurance certificate, I provide my

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: inspection certificate that I have a copy of with me, a hard copy just in case, and provide them all of that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: And basically they said to me, thank you very much for following the law, have a nice day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: But the second unit took me because of the electric assist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: And because of this, even despite that I provided all of my information, everything was completely on par, they took my bike and I lost about 20 days of work, which was a major hardship for me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: Because I'm a single father and I support not only my daughter, but her grandparents who take care of her.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: And so it's put me in a major position right now that I'm still trying to recuperate from.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: And so it's, you know, it's really hard for someone like myself who I do everything to make sure that when all my customers, it's always I agree.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: You agree, we go when it comes to pricing and when it comes to being completely transparent about everything that I do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: But for me to get hit in this manner is kind of really tough, knowing that, you know, during the stop, I saw five ripoff guys passing by with victims underway to getting ripped off.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: And they seem to continue to operate.

chapters.summary: Epstein notes recent e-bike safety hearings and resistance from DOT to allowing more electric assist. Winter says pedicabs need torque, not speed, average 6–10 mph in Central Park, and the industry has never had a pedicab-caused fatality; Camara says drivers need help, not speed.
chapters.title: Epstein asks panel to address electric-assist safety concerns

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And I know Councilman Brewer has a question.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: There's one more, just around the electric assist issue, because we've heard concerns.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We had a hearing, I think it was last week, I think it was, on e-bikes and e-bike safety and the proliferation of the problems in the city.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And so there's real resistance.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We've heard from DOT by allowing more.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Bikes to have electric assist.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: How do we respond to those safety concerns if we allow electric assist in this industry?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: To answer, Kenny is going to go ahead after you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: So really, for example, for us people that work in the park, for us it's really more of a torque thing, more an assistance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: There's not a real speed issue going on with pedicabs when it comes to Central Park, for example.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: The only thing that I'm concerned about when it comes to people driving a pedicab with an electric scissor, again, most of the guys that are in the Midtown area, the Times Square area, you know, over by Empire State Building and so on, they do a lot of these donuts

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: on the thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: Now, the industry has been around for 32 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: We've never had a fatality caused by a pedicab.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: We have a perfect safety record when it comes to this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: that the only time there's ever been a tragedy was caused by a reckless driver on 42nd Street, and that had nothing to do with the driver's operation of the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: I think that the 750 thing would be perfect because, I mean, really, it's really more about torque, not really about speed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: At least my maximum speed has been 14 miles an hour, and that's me trying really hard to do it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: Our average speed in Central Park, for example, is anywhere from 6 to 10 miles an hour.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: And so because we're doing tours, you know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Yeah, and I just can't even say it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: We're not looking for speed, you know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Again, we do a tour.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: People want to see things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: And so our concern is not about 15, 20 miles per hour.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: If you can even go five miles per hour, that would be fine.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Because people pay a lot of money to come to New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: They want to see things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: And we have people here like 67 years old, 60 years old.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: They're not looking for speed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: They just need help because if you have to pull three people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: And again, you know, most major cities now in everywhere, Asia, Africa, Europe, they have electric assist except New York City, which is the best city in the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: And they still not allow us to use that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: And that's kind of something need to be changed.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: All of the bikes have it or nearly all the bikes already have it.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: And all that's happening is people like Kenny are having their bikes confiscated, having their lives impacted.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: But it doesn't actually change whether.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: The drivers are driving with pedal assist.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks why pedicab batteries have not caused apartment fires like other e-bike batteries. Winter says street operators often charge batteries unsafely or buy cheap defective batteries, but garages now restrict charging; he supports UL certification and safe equipment.
chapters.title: Brewer asks panel about pedicab battery fire risks

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Councilmember Brewer?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: For whatever reason, the good news is that the pedicabs have not had fires in your apartments due to batteries.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And that's been mostly individuals.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What's the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I mean, I don't think you've had any.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You don't bring the pedicab home.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Explain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: So I know it's probably going to sound like I'm deriding them and stuff, but it's a hard truth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: A lot of the guys that work the street, they are, again, their number one thing is to get out there and work as long as possible, and they basically sometimes, you know, abuse their equipment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: And so what they care about is basically charging that battery as fast as possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: And very often they basically plug the batteries into the same outlets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: They have very unsafe practices sometimes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: Or the batteries are defective or they buy a cheaper battery because it's about cost.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: So nobody really does the research when it comes to this thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: So this is part of the reason why some of the fires happened.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: A lot of these things have been addressed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: And garages don't really allow anybody to charge their batteries in the garages anymore.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: No one will do it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: But why has it happened in somebody's home?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: But it's probably because of that very same reason.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: They finally started to wake up and do the right thing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I think if we work on the industry as a whole, then licensing batteries will be the correct battery.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That's also part of the...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: L certification really goes a long way with that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: You know, I personally have never, ever had an incident because I do my research and make sure that what I buy is high quality to make sure that I'm never going to have that issue because I never want to have my name attached to something like that,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: which is part of something that I was concerned about when my bikes were actually confiscated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: When the officers took my bikes, the batteries were still connected, and I was really worried that when they ended up at 41st Street, they have a lot there where they keep the bikes, that they would react with the rain because I don't ride in the rain and I don't work the street.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: So I was worried that it was going to rain that weekend and I was worried that it was going to have a reaction as it did on 48th Street.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: There was a fire on 48th Street in an open air lot when someone left a defective battery in the rain, which reacted and then caused a major problem there.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: And one more thing to just add to what Kenny said.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: You know, outside right here, we have like a place where they're charging a bunch of, you know, battery and stuff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: I think this thing, this is not to us, it's not even an issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: We're okay as an IPA, you know, our perspective, whatever the safety measures are available, we'll use that because our concern is pretty much the safety because we're all family members and stuff like that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: We care deeply about that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: So we're open to anything, you know, in order to make sure everybody's safe.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks how the city could enforce pedicab laws without criminal summonses. Mendez says TLC could issue civil tickets tied to the cab owner and license, making violations an industry issue rather than a criminal one.
chapters.title: Brewer asks Mendez how to enforce pedicab laws civilly

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: One quick question for Michelle.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How could the city effectively enforce pedicab laws without relying on criminal summonses?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You talked about that a little bit, if you could expand.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: Sure, I think I do.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: It would be under TLC.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: They would have street-level enforcement that's civil in nature.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: They could give tickets for the top charges that I named, like having a...

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: You know, taillight out and it would be tied to the owner of the cab.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: It would be tied to the pedicab license.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Mendez
utterances.text: It would be an industry issue as opposed to a criminal one.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks whether the panel supports moving pedicab oversight to TLC. Camara says the alliance is open to any agency but wants answers on fitness requirements and insurance; Winter says they are open to solutions without unintended consequences.
chapters.title: Brewer asks public panel if they support TLC oversight

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do all of you support moving the industry to TLC?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Is that a general positive reaction?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: Yes, we, as I said from my speech, we are open to work with any agency, but at the same time, you know, our members just want more information about TLC, you know, like, you know, because there are a few questions that our members are asking, and then

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: we want to make sure about those, like, for example, the fitness requirement in the bill, and the fact that the TLC also might be able to kind of increase the insurance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: So there are a couple of questions that we want to make sure, and we don't have an answer to give to our members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: We want to make sure we got all the answers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Makan Camara
utterances.text: But we 100% want to work with any agency to make sure the enforcement is there and then the public, everybody is safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: We're open to any solutions as long as they don't have a double-edged sword effect, you know, and unintended consequences that's going to negatively affect our members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: You know, so long as it's, you know, moving forward in a positive way and constructive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: We are definitely open to pretty much anything.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and thank you for your service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Christine Nicholas, chair of the Broadway Association, says she is not opposed to pedicabs but the industry lacks clear regulation and creates safety and consumer risks. She supports Intros 992, 673, 77, 993, and 1026, and urges the Council to consolidate the seven bills into a clear law.
chapters.title: Christine Nicholas of Broadway Association supports pedicab reform bills

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you for this panel.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And the next panel is, thank you, David Satinstall, Tom Harris, and Christine Nichols.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Whenever you're ready, you can start.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: Yeah, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenneth Winter
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Nicholas
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Epstein and members of the Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Nicholas
utterances.text: My name is Christine Nicholas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Nicholas
utterances.text: I am the chair of the 115-year-old New York City business institution, the Broadway Association, dedicated to the betterment of the Broadway corridor from 14th Street up to Columbus Circle, encompassing Times Square and the Theater District.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Nicholas
utterances.text: First off, I wanted to just say that I am not personally opposed to the pedicab industry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Nicholas
utterances.text: I have used pedicabs because I am the mom of three kids that have insisted on using the pedicabs every now and then.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Nicholas
utterances.text: Thank you for your understanding and your interest in fixing the pedicab industry that operates without clear regulations, obviously from the testimony, the majority of which are unlicensed, creating safety risks

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Nicholas
utterances.text: for passengers and pedestrians, an unsafe environment for the city's busiest areas, Broadway and the end time square.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Nicholas
utterances.text: And for consumers, especially tourists, the vague pricing has made rip-offs and overcharging a common occurrence with no repercussions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Nicholas
utterances.text: The seven bills under consideration represent common-sense solutions agreed upon by the industry advocates, the Midtown Bid Coalition and the Midtown Community Justice Center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Nicholas
utterances.text: Having seven separate bills is affirmation that this industry is in desperate need of reform, yet seven separate bills are also confusing to the public, and we urge the City Council to simplify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Nicholas
utterances.text: this process and consolidate these bills to pass a law that promotes safety, transparency, accountability, and fairness to all of those affected and involved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Nicholas
utterances.text: Regarding the specific legislation under consideration today, the Broadway Association supports Intro 992, Intro 0673, and Intro 0077.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Nicholas
utterances.text: To standardize rates and mandate meters requiring visible pricing, scannable registration plates with information about the pedicab business owner, and prohibiting amplified sound.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Nicholas
utterances.text: The Broadway Association supports interim 993 moving oversight and DCWP to the TLC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Nicholas
utterances.text: Which could fix the broken link between licensing and enforcement in Intro 1026 to designate curb space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Nicholas
utterances.text: Just in closing, the bills under consideration underscore the need for immediate action, but like any rules, any new rules or laws, they're only as good as the enforcement required to put them into effect.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Nicholas
utterances.text: We strongly suggest that if the TLC is successful in getting oversight,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Nicholas
utterances.text: Although it doesn't sound like they want it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Nicholas
utterances.text: We also urge that the 24-7 NYPD remain involved in enforcing unlawful and dangerous behavior that has made Midtown seem chaotic and ungovernable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christine Nicholas
utterances.text: The Broadway Association thanks the chair and Councilwoman Gail Brewer and the committee for making this a priority.

chapters.summary: David Saltonstall, VP at the Central Park Conservancy, supports the reform package and TLC oversight. He says nearly every out-of-town visitor near Central Park is aggressively solicited, and Grand Army Plaza and Columbus Circle often feel like a shakedown with unclear fares.
chapters.title: David Saltonstall of Central Park Conservancy describes pedicab shakedowns

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, whoever's next, whatever.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You guys can just decide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Saltonstall
utterances.text: Good morning, members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Saltonstall
utterances.text: My name is David Saltonstall, and I'm Vice President of Government Relations and Policy at the Central Park Conservancy, and thank you for this opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Saltonstall
utterances.text: The Conservancy supports this package of bills to reform the city's pedicab fleet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Saltonstall
utterances.text: Moving oversight to the TLC, requiring meters or timers in every pedicab, and making it possible to weed out bad actors are common sense steps.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Saltonstall
utterances.text: But rather than walking through each bill, I want to describe what the current system looks like from our perspective.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Saltonstall
utterances.text: Central Park is the city's most visited attraction with more than 40 million visits a year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Saltonstall
utterances.text: And virtually every visitor from out of town is solicited, often aggressively, by a small subset of pedicab operators or their agents within a few blocks of the park.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Saltonstall
utterances.text: Not some of them, nearly all of them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Saltonstall
utterances.text: For many, it's confusing, and too often it ends with a sky-high fare that was never made clear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Saltonstall
utterances.text: A family told one price at the outset and charged several times that amount at the end of the ride.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Saltonstall
utterances.text: Grand Army Plaza and Columbus Circle were designed as grand entrances to one of the world's most iconic green spaces.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Saltonstall
utterances.text: Instead, those areas feel more like a shakedown.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Saltonstall
utterances.text: That's the first impression many visitors get of Central Park, and it's a memory they take home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Saltonstall
utterances.text: It reflects on the park, and it reflects on New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Saltonstall
utterances.text: It doesn't have to be this way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Saltonstall
utterances.text: Pedicabs can be a safe, green, and genuinely enjoyable way to see the park.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Saltonstall
utterances.text: What we need is a well-regulated fleet, one that rewards the many honest drivers who are simply trying to make a living, some of whom you've heard from today, and rids the industry of those whose business model depends on exploiting people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Saltonstall
utterances.text: Who don't know better.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Saltonstall
utterances.text: A properly regulated fleet under the TLC can also be managed so it has minimal impact on the park's already crowded drives, which are shared by cyclists, runners, and millions of others.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Saltonstall
utterances.text: Finally, I do want to recognize the New York Pedicab Alliance, whose members have spoken here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Saltonstall
utterances.text: I imagine it is a rare event when this body is asked to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Saltonstall
utterances.text: regulate an industry when the members of that industry come up and are literally begging you for more reform, for more oversight.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Saltonstall
utterances.text: They welcome it because they know it protects their livelihoods as much as it protects the public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Saltonstall
utterances.text: So we urge the council to pass this package in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Saltonstall
utterances.text: And I'd be happy to answer any questions.

chapters.summary: Tom Harris, president of the Times Square Alliance, says pedicabs are vehicles for hire and should be regulated by TLC. He argues criminal summonses are ineffective, civil penalties tied to licenses would create accountability, and pedicabs should be allowed electric assist.
chapters.title: Tom Harris of Times Square Alliance calls for TLC oversight and civil penalties

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: My name is Tom Harris, president of the Times Square Alliance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: I want to thank Chairman Epstein, Council Member Brewer, members of the committee, and members of the council for helping to make the pedicab industry work for all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: A pedicab ride can be a nice way to see our great city, or it can be a noisy experience that ends with a huge unexpected cost.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: The choice is ours.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: For far too long, the pedicab industry has not worked for the community, for the consumers, and we found out for most of the honest drivers themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: Most of them are honest, like Kenny and McCann.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: They're just working people looking to make a living.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: Those honest workers are overshadowed by another group who flouts the laws and takes advantage of consumers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: First, let's look at what pedicabs do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: Pedicabs pick people up, take them somewhere, and charge them money.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: The very definition of a vehicle for hire.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: But for reasons most of us can't remember, they're not regulated by the Taxi and Limousine Commission, the entity that regulates vehicles for hire and does a great job.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: Right now, DCWP licenses the pedicabs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: The NYPD enforces the laws through a mix of civil and ineffective criminal court summonses, most of which are dismissed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: There's no connection between the summons and the licenses, no accountability for owners of the pedicabs and bad actors, making it difficult for good actors to remain compliant and still make a living.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: In partnership with the Pedicab Alliance, the Central Park Conservancy, the Midtown Justice Center, and the Times Square Alliance, we developed recommendations

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: reflected in this legislation that will treat pedicabs like other vehicles for hire with fixed fares, meters, visible identification,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: civil penalties attached to licenses, a prohibition for amplified sound under the jurisdiction of the TLC, with a strong recommendation to increase the staffing of the TLC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: There's been a lot of talk about resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: A great deal of resources are currently dedicated to enforcing pedicab laws.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: They're just ineffective and put in the wrong place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: We also support pedicabs being allowed to have electric assist power.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: Other cities have been able to regulate pedicabs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: There's no reason New York City, the greatest city in the world, can't do the same thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: Once again, thank you.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks the panel for specific steps to license more pedicab drivers. Harris says criminal court summonses are the wrong tool because discovery and jail exposure lead to dismissals; civil summonses with seizure authority would create accountability and bring compliance.
chapters.title: Brewer asks panel how to bring pedicab drivers into licensing

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you, and I want to acknowledge I've been joined by Councilmember Krishnan, and Councilmember Brewer, I'll let you go first this time.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: My question is, given the fact that you know better than anybody else, perhaps, what the challenges are of the...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Possibilities for the future with the Taxi Limousine Commission if we're able to pull that off.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How specifically would you suggest we get some of these individuals licensed?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In other words, you have the bills in front of you, but you know more than I think most of us about what you might be more specific about how to make the industry better in the hopes, too, that TLC takes over.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But that's not the– there's many steps that would have to be included.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I was wondering if you could suggest some of them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: So the first thing is the New York City Police Department does a great job.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: They're utility players, and they're expected to enforce all sorts of laws.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: Criminal court summons is their forte.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: That's not the place where these summonses should be heard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: First off, when you issue a criminal court summons, discovery kicks in, there's jail time applied.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: We shouldn't be sending people to jail for doing their work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: So the problem is that these summonses are dismissed because the police cannot comply with the discovery components.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: For an offense that requires jail time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: So anything that they do for unlicensed drivers is ineffective because like Kenny and McCann said, a couple of days later they get back their pedicab.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: If this was regulated civilly, and whoever regulates it civilly, it could be a combination, but if the police department or the TLC or any other agency issued a civil summons,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: They could seize the pedicab for an unlicensed operator.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: They would be found guilty because the discovery or the standard of proof is different than in the criminal court.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: So in my opinion,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: That would bring compliance in line because you have accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tom Harris
utterances.text: Right now, there's zero accountability for any of the summonses issued, and that's why the enforcement to date has been ineffective.

chapters.summary: Adamu Mazalu, a 53-year-old driver from Niger living in the Bronx, says pedicabbing has been his American dream for almost 10 years. He has arthritis in both knees and asks the Council to support Intro 1063 so he can keep working with pedal assist.

utterances.text: I have been working as a pedicab driver on the street since 2007.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenan Duzenli
utterances.text: I am here to strongly support Intro 126 to create dedicated relief stands.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenan Duzenli
utterances.text: Over the 19 years, I've been firsthand why this infrastructure is desperately needed, not just for the drivers, but for the entire city, especially in our busiest touristic place like Midtown and Times Square.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenan Duzenli
utterances.text: First, this bill protects customer parking and meter revenue in high-demand areas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenan Duzenli
utterances.text: Currently, without designated zones, pedicabs have to take up standard metered spaces while waiting for fares.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenan Duzenli
utterances.text: By putting pedicabs specifically in designated curb spaces,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenan Duzenli
utterances.text: The city gets functional commercial staging around Times Square.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenan Duzenli
utterances.text: Second, it reduces mid-street traffic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenan Duzenli
utterances.text: When we don't have a dedicated pull-off spot in heavy midtown traffic, drivers are forced to double park in the active lanes just to load and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenan Duzenli
utterances.text: unload passengers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenan Duzenli
utterances.text: A marked designated curb space gets our pedicabs completely out of the traffic flow, instantly preventing gridlock behind us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenan Duzenli
utterances.text: Third, Intro 1026 eliminates pedestrian conflict in heavily foot traffic

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenan Duzenli
utterances.text: Places operated without official stands often have to idle near crosswalks or cluster near hotel doors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenan Duzenli
utterances.text: Dedicated stand confine operators to a predictable footprint.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenan Duzenli
utterances.text: Fourth, this is an exceptional low-cost fix.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenan Duzenli
utterances.text: It only requires painting and signing on the curb to immediately clear up congested intersections in the heart of the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenan Duzenli
utterances.text: Finally, these zones will significantly streamline enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenan Duzenli
utterances.text: Right now, citing drivers for blocking the roadway creates legal gray areas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kenan Duzenli
utterances.text: With explicit designated spaces, enforcement officers will have clear-cut boundaries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Councilmember Epstein, Councilmember Brewer, everybody watching remotely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen
utterances.text: My name is Christina Hansen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen
utterances.text: I am a New York City carriage driver.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen
utterances.text: I'm a licensed sightseeing guide, and I'm a longtime resident of Hell's Kitchen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen
utterances.text: So I've been an observer of the pedicab industry for a long, long time, as it's immediately adjacent to my line of work and in my neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen
utterances.text: And I would like to say, first of all, I agree with the Conservancy very much about their observations about what goes on in the park.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen
utterances.text: Central Park South has become utterly degraded with aggressive ticket selling and things like that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen
utterances.text: Also, though, there are a lot of good operators in the park.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen
utterances.text: Right now, with everything else that's going on in the park, they do operate safely and slowly at 6 to 10 miles an hour.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen
utterances.text: They're not going 15 miles an hour.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen
utterances.text: They're not going 30 miles an hour with that electric assist, which, although it is currently illegal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen
utterances.text: That being said, I heard a lot of questions from the committee to the administration about what sort of technology could we employ here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen
utterances.text: And the technology that's not being employed here is a very simple one, and it's called a license plate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen
utterances.text: They talk about plates on pedicabs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen
utterances.text: But it is just a sticker on the fork of the vehicle that it's a sticker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen
utterances.text: And if it peels off, it's voided.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen
utterances.text: So the pedicab operators are kind of forced to put zip ties around it so nobody could peel it off and ruin their plate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen
utterances.text: You can't read it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen
utterances.text: It's a four-digit number.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen
utterances.text: They can be covered up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen
utterances.text: There's only 840 plates out there and only 340 being issued right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen
utterances.text: You know, yellow cabs right now have a light on the top.

utterances.text: It's like a very short number.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen
utterances.text: They've got a plate from TLC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christina Hansen

summary: The Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection held a hearing on seven bills to reform pedicab regulation, covering theater-district restrictions, timers, fares, meters, TLC oversight, curb space, and electric assist.
DCWP and TLC testified about licensing, enforcement gaps, unlicensed operators, insurance costs, and concerns over transferring pedicab oversight to TLC.

Public witnesses, including drivers, advocates, the Broadway Association, Central Park Conservancy, and Times Square Alliance, described overcharging and safety issues, with many drivers urging legalization of pedal assist.

topic: Restrictions on the operation of pedicabs in the theatre district zone
